[2026-15181: lines 1322-1661 of 4520, FR page 47328]
  1322  III. USTR Responses to Significant Comments
  1323  
  1324      In response to the June 5, 2026 FRN, USTR received over 1,600 
  1325  written comments and heard testimony from over 100 witnesses. USTR and 
  1326  the Section 301 Committee reviewed, examined, and considered each 
  1327  comment and the public testimony. USTR responds below to significant 
  1328  issues raised in the public comments and hearings in response to the 
  1329  June 5, 2026 FRN and further explains the Trade Representative's 
  1330  determinations to take appropriate and feasible action under Section 
  1331  301(b) at the specific direction of the President. See 19 U.S.C. 
  1332  2411(b)(2).
  1333  
  1334  A. Response to Comments Regarding Prior Determinations on Actionability
  1335  
  1336      Multiple comments raised arguments taking issue with some or all of 
  1337  the conclusions the Trade Representative reached in his actionability 
  1338  finding and Report in these investigations. These include arguments 
  1339  that the Trade Representative failed to substantiate the existence of 
  1340  unreasonable acts, policies, or practices in each investigation, or 
  1341  that the Trade Representative failed to demonstrate a burden or 
  1342  restriction imposed by the acts, policies, and practices of each 
  1343  economy. With respect to these arguments and other arguments regarding 
  1344  the Trade Representative's earlier findings on actionability, the Trade 
  1345  Representative observes that any such arguments that were appropriately 
  1346  raised during the actionability phase of these investigations were 
  1347  addressed in the June 5, 2026 FRN or the related comprehensive Report. 
  1348  Moreover, the Trade Representative has taken into account all available 
  1349  information regarding the efforts of the investigated economies to 
  1350  impose and effectively enforce forced labor import prohibitions since 
  1351  the issuance of the June 5, 2026 FRN.
  1352  
  1353  B. Comments Regarding the Use of Tariffs and Tariff Rates
  1354  
  1355  1. Responses to Significant Comments Regarding the Appropriateness of 
  1356  the Additional Tariffs To Address the Acts, Policies, and Practices 
  1357  Under Investigation
  1358      A number of comments argued that the additional tariffs proposed in 
  1359  these investigations are not appropriate to achieve the elimination of 
  1360  the unreasonable acts, policies, or practices of each of the 
  1361  investigated economies. These comments argued, among other things, that 
  1362  additional tariffs would be unlikely to significantly lessen the use of 
  1363  forced labor. Other comments argued
  1364  
  1365  [[Page 47329]]
  1366  
  1367  that USTR should undertake diplomatic engagement or engage in technical 
  1368  assistance and capacity building in order to achieve the elimination of 
  1369  the acts, policies, or practices in these investigations.
  1370      With respect to the first argument, consistent with the specific 
  1371  direction of the President, the Trade Representative has determined to 
  1372  impose tariffs as a means to encourage the investigated economies to 
  1373  impose and effectively enforce a forced labor import ban. Further, USTR 
  1374  observes that since the initiation of the investigations and the 
  1375  announcement of the proposed tariff actions, various economies have 
  1376  imposed or are taking steps toward imposing a forced labor import 
  1377  prohibition. This serves to confirm that tariff action can help obtain 
  1378  the elimination of the investigated acts, policies, and practices. 
  1379  While the elimination of forced labor generally is not the aim of these 
  1380  Section 301 investigations, as observed in the Report, the prevalence 
  1381  of forced labor has increased in recent years. Existing efforts to 
  1382  address forced labor have proven inadequate to prevent this increase. 
  1383  As discussed in the Report in these investigations, it is well 
  1384  established that an effectively enforced forced labor import 
  1385  prohibition can lead to the remediation of significant instances of 
  1386  forced labor.
  1387      With respect to technical assistance and capacity building, we 
  1388  observe that such efforts on their own are unlikely to achieve the 
  1389  elimination of the unreasonable acts, policies, and practices. However, 
  1390  where an economy agrees to address the issue of forced labor imports, 
  1391  and seeks assistance to impose or effectively enforce such a 
  1392  prohibition, such activities will be more effective. As discussed 
  1393  above, trade-based measures, particularly tariffs, are encouraging 
  1394  economies to impose or take steps toward imposing a forced labor import 
  1395  prohibition.
  1396      While the Trade Representative has considered the arguments raised 
  1397  in the comments, the Trade Representative disagrees with the comments 
  1398  for the reasons discussed above. Furthermore, because the comments 
  1399  suggested alternative actions that are inconsistent with the specific 
  1400  direction of the President, the Trade Representative cannot accommodate 
  1401  them.
  1402  2. Response to Comments Regarding the Proposed Tariff Rates
  1403      USTR received several types of comments regarding the proposed 
  1404  rates of duty for each investigation. For example, multiple comments 
  1405  questioned whether a 10 or 12.5 percent duty would be significant 
  1406  enough to encourage economies to eliminate the investigated acts, 
  1407  policies, and practices. Some comments argued that the 2.5 percentage 
  1408  point difference between the two rates is not significant enough to 
  1409  encourage economies to eliminate the investigated acts, policies, or 
  1410  practices. Multiple comments argued for certain investigated economies 
  1411  to be excluded from the application of additional duties or be assigned 
  1412  a lower additional rate of duty, including where the economy has 
  1413  domestic laws prohibiting forced labor. Related to these arguments, 
  1414  certain other comments argued that it was not appropriate for economies 
  1415  that have made commitments regarding forced labor in ARTs to receive 
  1416  the same tariff rate as economies with a forced labor import 
  1417  prohibition, or economies that have taken steps towards enforcement of 
  1418  a forced labor import prohibition, or economies with partial regimes 
  1419  with the effect of preventing the importation of certain forced labor 
  1420  goods. USTR addresses each of these comments in turn.
  1421      With respect to the significance of the rates of duty in these 
  1422  investigations, including the differential of 2.5 percentage points, 
  1423  the Trade Representative has determined that the rate for each economy 
  1424  is appropriate to obtain the elimination of that economy's acts, 
  1425  policies, and practices at this time. The Trade Representative 
  1426  considers that a lower rate of duty would not be appropriate to obtain 
  1427  the elimination of the acts, policies, and practices, at this time. The 
  1428  specific action and level of duty that will obtain the elimination of 
  1429  an act, policy, or practice is a matter of judgment, to be exercised by 
  1430  the Trade Representative, subject to any specific direction of the 
  1431  President. Information available indicates that these tariff rates and 
  1432  the differential between them are significant enough to spur action by 
  1433  investigated economies. Since the publication of the proposed actions 
  1434  in these investigations, a number of economies have either imposed 
  1435  forced labor import prohibitions, or undertaken a commitment to impose 
  1436  a forced labor import prohibition as part of an ART. Other economies 
  1437  have informed USTR that they are in the process of developing such 
  1438  measures. Accordingly, the rates and the differential between them have 
  1439  been successful in encouraging investigated economies to take steps 
  1440  toward eliminating the investigated acts, policies, and practices.
  1441      With respect to excluding economies or providing a lower rate of 
  1442  duty based on those economies' efforts to address forced labor within 
  1443  their jurisdictions, such as the ratification of International Labor 
  1444  Organization (ILO) conventions or domestic enforcement efforts related 
  1445  to forced labor, doing so would not achieve the elimination of the 
  1446  investigated acts, policies, and practices. The Trade Representative 
  1447  applauds the efforts of our trading partners to eliminate forced labor 
  1448  within their jurisdictions; however, as discussed in our June 5, 2026 
  1449  FRN and the related Report, these efforts are not pertinent to the 
  1450  elimination of the acts, policies, and practices that are the subject 
  1451  of these investigations.
  1452      With respect to excluding or providing a lower rate to economies 
  1453  that are in the process of developing forced labor import prohibitions, 
  1454  the mere development or proposal of a measure to prohibit the 
  1455  importation of forced labor goods, absent adoption of such measure, is 
  1456  insufficient to address the acts, policies, and practices that are the 
  1457  subject of these investigations. The development or proposal of such 
  1458  measures alone provides no guarantee that a forced labor import 
  1459  prohibition will be adopted and effectively enforced. Further, this is 
  1460  distinct from circumstances where an economy has taken on a concrete 
  1461  obligation to prohibit the importation of goods. Certain comments 
  1462  contend that the Trade Representative should assign different rates of 
  1463  duty to each of the following groups of economies: (1) those that have 
  1464  imposed forced labor import prohibitions; (2) those that made 
  1465  commitments regarding forced labor in an ART or other similar 
  1466  agreement; and (3) those that have imposed a partial regime with the 
  1467  effect of preventing the importation of certain forced labor goods. In 
  1468  the Trade Representative's judgment, imposing distinct tariff rates on 
  1469  each of these groups at this time would hinder the ability of the Trade 
  1470  Representative to achieve the elimination of the investigated acts, 
  1471  policies, and practices. The Trade Representative's determination to 
  1472  apply a lower rate of duty to each economy meeting these criteria 
  1473  acknowledges significant steps such economies are taking toward 
  1474  imposing and effectively enforcing forced labor import prohibitions.
  1475      Considering the public comments and the advice of the Section 301 
  1476  Committee, as well as the advice of advisory committees, and consistent 
  1477  with the specific direction of the President, the Trade Representative 
  1478  has determined that it is appropriate to impose tariffs of 10 percent 
  1479  or 10 percent net of MFN duties, based on whether an economy has 
  1480  imposed a
  1481  
  1482  [[Page 47330]]
  1483  
  1484  forced labor import prohibition, has undertaken commitments in an ART 
  1485  regarding forced labor import prohibition, or has imposed a partial 
  1486  regime with the effect of preventing the importation of certain forced 
  1487  labor goods, and has determined that it is appropriate to impose 
  1488  tariffs of 12.5 percent or 12.5 percent net of MFN duties for each 
  1489  other investigated economy. In the Trade Representative's judgment, 
  1490  imposing an economy-wide rate of zero or lower than 10 percent on 
  1491  economies that have entered into an ART without implementing a forced 
  1492  labor import prohibition, or on economies that have imposed a 
  1493  prohibition but do not yet effectively implement such prohibition, 
  1494  would be ineffective in encouraging the elimination of the acts, 
  1495  policies, and practices under investigation. While the Trade 
  1496  Representative has considered the arguments raised in the comments, the 
  1497  Trade Representative disagrees with the comments for the reasons 
  1498  discussed above. Furthermore, because the comments suggested 
  1499  alternative actions that are inconsistent with the specific direction 
  1500  of the President, the Trade Representative cannot accommodate them.
  1501  3. Response to Comments Urging Lower Tariff Rates in Investigations of 
  1502  Economies With Perceived Low-Risk Supply
  1503      Multiple comments suggested that the Trade Representative should 
  1504  impose a lower or zero tariff rate on economies with export industries 
  1505  that have a low-risk of forced labor in their supply chains. For 
  1506  example, certain commenters argued that where investigated economies 
  1507  export products to major U.S. retailers with their own supply chain due 
  1508  diligence procedures, additional tariffs on such products would be 
  1509  ineffective in bringing about the elimination of the investigated acts, 
  1510  policies, and practices. These comments misunderstand the aims of the 
  1511  investigations and the use of tariffs as leverage.
  1512      As demonstrated throughout the investigations, including in the 
  1513  Report, the investigations are broader than any particular industry or 
  1514  supply chain. The aim of each investigation is to encourage that 
  1515  economy to impose and effectively enforce a forced labor import 
  1516  prohibition. As already seen in certain investigations to date, tariffs 
  1517  have proved to be an effective point of leverage to encourage the 
  1518  elimination of the investigated acts, policies, and practices. Even 
  1519  accepting these arguments at face value, it does not follow that U.S. 
  1520  products do not compete in those economies against other imports 
  1521  manufactured with forced labor, or that other exports from those 
  1522  economies (i.e., those not subject to supply chain due diligence 
  1523  procedures) are not manufactured with imported inputs made with forced 
  1524  labor. While the Trade Representative has considered the arguments 
  1525  raised in the comments, the Trade Representative disagrees with the 
  1526  comments for the reasons discussed above. Furthermore, because the 
  1527  comments suggested alternative actions that are inconsistent with the 
  1528  specific direction of the President, the Trade Representative cannot 
  1529  accommodate them.
  1530  
  1531  C. Discussion of Comments on Proposed Product Exemptions
  1532  
  1533      USTR received a variety of comments on the proposed exemption list, 
  1534  including support for the products proposed for exemption and requests 
  1535  to remove certain products from the proposed exemption list. 
  1536  Considering the public comments and the advice of the Section 301 
  1537  Committee, as well as the advice of advisory committees and in 
  1538  accordance with the specific direction of the President, the Trade 
  1539  Representative has determined to exempt all of the products proposed 
  1540  for exemption in Annex A to the June 5, 2026 FRN, except the non-
  1541  pharmaceutical applications of certain chemical products. Other than 
  1542  the products with non-pharmaceutical applications, as discussed below, 
  1543  the Trade Representative determined not to remove additional products 
  1544  from the exemption list. The Trade Representative determined to exempt 
  1545  certain additional products not included in the proposed exemptions in 
  1546  Annex A to June 5, 2026 FRN.
  1547  1. Support for Keeping Products on the Proposed Exemption List
  1548      USTR received a number of comments expressing support for 
  1549  maintaining certain proposed exemptions. Comments supported the 
  1550  exemption of coffee, mineral tars, certain copper products, iron 
  1551  oxides, coke, aluminum oxide, and coconut products. Other comments 
  1552  expressed support for maintaining the proposed exemptions from Section 
  1553  301 tariffs for products that are subject to Section 232 tariffs. 
  1554  Commenters generally noted that these products are raw materials with 
  1555  limited-to-no availability from domestic sources or cannot be grown or 
  1556  produced in sufficient quantities or at reasonable prices in the United 
  1557  States or obtained from other sources.
  1558      Considering the public comments and the advice of the Section 301 
  1559  Committee, as well as the advice of advisory committees--and in 
  1560  accordance with the specific direction of the President--the Trade 
  1561  Representative has determined not to remove products other than the 
  1562  non-pharmaceutical applications of certain products from the proposed 
  1563  exemption list, as the remaining products in the proposed exemption 
  1564  list constitute: (1) raw materials that if subject to the proposed 
  1565  additional tariffs could lead to the unavailability of domestic supply; 
  1566  (2) products that could cause economy-wide disruptions if subject to 
  1567  the proposed additional tariffs; (3) products that cannot be grown or 
  1568  produced in sufficient quantities or at reasonable prices in the United 
  1569  States or obtained from other sources; or (4) products for which 
  1570  tariffs may not contribute substantially to the elimination of the 
  1571  acts, policies, and practices found to be actionable.
  1572  2. Determination To Remove Certain Products From the Proposed Exemption 
  1573  List
  1574      Considering the public comments and the advice of the Section 301 
  1575  Committee, as well as the advice of advisory committees--and in 
  1576  accordance with the specific direction of the President--the Trade 
  1577  Representative has determined to limit the exemption for certain 
  1578  chemicals and chemical products to their pharmaceutical applications. 
  1579  Certain comments noted the health-related applications of products 
  1580  proposed for exemptions and stated that certain ingredients that 
  1581  support U.S. manufacturing of healthcare products are not available in 
  1582  the United States in sufficient quantities to meet domestic demand. 
  1583  Some commenters also requested that these product exemptions be limited 
  1584  to their pharmaceutical applications due to competition with domestic 
  1585  production. Limiting exemptions for these proposed chemical products to 
  1586  their pharmaceutical applications is consistent with the proposal in 
  1587  the June 5, 2026 FRN because an exemption for all applications is 
  1588  broader than necessary to cover goods that have limited availability 
  1589  outside of the investigated economies.
  1590  3. Comments Requesting the Removal of Additional Products From 
  1591  Exemption List
  1592      Some commenters requested that USTR remove other products from the 
  1593  proposed exemption list or otherwise advocated for narrowly tailored 
  1594  exemptions. Industries or products for which commenters expressed
  1595  
  1596  [[Page 47331]]
  1597  
  1598  opposition to proposed exemptions include beef, avocados, paprika and 
  1599  paprika products, lithium hexafluorophosphate, and forgings and 
  1600  articles containing forgings.
  1601      Commenters suggested, for example, that beef imported from certain 
  1602  economies is linked to certain acts, policies, and practices found 
  1603  actionable in these investigations, and that exempting these products 
  1604  would benefit foreign exporters of beef produced with forced labor at 
  1605  the expense of the American cattle producer. Similarly, commenters 
  1606  suggested that paprika and paprika derived products, lithium 
  1607  hexafluorophosphate, and certain chemicals used in the production of 
  1608  pesticides are imported from certain economies linked to certain acts, 
  1609  policies, and practices found actionable in these investigations.
  1610      Additionally, commenters suggested that imports of these products 
  1611  are available from domestic sources and are putting pressure on 
  1612  domestic producers. With respect to paprika and paprika derived 
  1613  products, commenters suggested that imports have caused market 
  1614  disruptions, preventing U.S. production of these products. 
  1615  Additionally, comments reported that imports of lithium 
  1616  hexafluorophosphate and certain chemicals used in the production of 
  1617  pesticides have inhibited U.S. production of these products. Commenters 
  1618  pointed to recent and anticipated expansion in U.S. production 
  1619  capabilities, and suggested that imposing tariffs on these products 
  1620  could support investment and employment in domestic production. With 
  1621  respect to forgings and articles containing forgings, commenters 
  1622  suggested that these products are readily available from domestic 
  1623  sources, at reasonable prices, in sufficient quantities and that 
  1624  subjecting imports of these products to tariffs could support 
  1625  investment and employment in the United States. Similarly, comments 
  1626  suggested that the domestic avocado industry is under significant 
  1627  pressure due to low-priced avocado imports and applying tariffs would 
  1628  benefit certain U.S. agricultural producers.
  1629      Considering the public comments and the advice of the Section 301 
  1630  Committee, as well as the advice of advisory committees--and in 
  1631  accordance with the specific direction of the President--the Trade 
  1632  Representative has determined not to remove these products from the 
  1633  list of exempted products. There remains limited availability of these 
  1634  products from domestic sources, a point conceded by one commenter 
  1635  regarding paprika. Regarding claims that these products should be 
  1636  subject to the tariffs because they are related to acts, policies, and 
  1637  practices found actionable in these investigations, Section 
  1638  301(c)(3)(B) provides that the Trade Representative is authorized to 
  1639  take action against any goods or economic sector ``without regard to 
  1640  whether or not such goods or economic sector were involved in the act, 
  1641  policy, or practice that is the subject of such action.''
  1642  
  1643  D. Determination To Exempt Additional Products
  1644  
  1645      In addition to the products initially proposed for exemption in the 
  1646  June 5, 2026 FRN, the Trade Representative, in accordance with the 
  1647  specific direction of the President, has determined in each 
  1648  investigation to exclude an additional 471 products from tariffs 
  1649  imposed with respect to products of that economy. In certain 
  1650  investigations, the Trade Representative also has determined to apply 
  1651  additional exemptions for products from that specific investigated 
  1652  economy based on requested exemptions negotiated in the context of 
  1653  certain agreements and arrangements.
  1654      A number of comments expressed support for product exemptions in 
  1655  addition to the initial list of proposed exemptions in the June 5, 2026 
  1656  FRN. Comments requested exemptions of products including certain 
  1657  agriculture products; metals and alloys; chemicals; semiconductor 
  1658  manufacturing equipment; and art, antique, and collectible products. 
  1659  Certain economies that have concluded ARTs or similar arrangements with 
  1660  the United States have also requested exemption of products negotiated 
  1661  as part of those agreements and arrangements.

[2026-15181: lines 1643-1942 of 4520, FR page 47331]
  1643  D. Determination To Exempt Additional Products
  1644  
  1645      In addition to the products initially proposed for exemption in the 
  1646  June 5, 2026 FRN, the Trade Representative, in accordance with the 
  1647  specific direction of the President, has determined in each 
  1648  investigation to exclude an additional 471 products from tariffs 
  1649  imposed with respect to products of that economy. In certain 
  1650  investigations, the Trade Representative also has determined to apply 
  1651  additional exemptions for products from that specific investigated 
  1652  economy based on requested exemptions negotiated in the context of 
  1653  certain agreements and arrangements.
  1654      A number of comments expressed support for product exemptions in 
  1655  addition to the initial list of proposed exemptions in the June 5, 2026 
  1656  FRN. Comments requested exemptions of products including certain 
  1657  agriculture products; metals and alloys; chemicals; semiconductor 
  1658  manufacturing equipment; and art, antique, and collectible products. 
  1659  Certain economies that have concluded ARTs or similar arrangements with 
  1660  the United States have also requested exemption of products negotiated 
  1661  as part of those agreements and arrangements.
  1662      Having considered the public comments, advice of the Section 301 
  1663  Committee, as well as the advice of advisory committees, and the 
  1664  specific direction of the President, the Trade Representative 
  1665  determined to exempt the following additional products from the scope 
  1666  of actions: certain animal products; certain seeds; certain vegetable 
  1667  products; certain sugar and sugar containing products; unflavored 
  1668  instant coffee; certain fertilizer inputs and pesticide inputs; certain 
  1669  animal hides and leather; certain wood products; vanadium oxides and 
  1670  hydroxides; pig iron; certain ferrous inputs and waste; certain 
  1671  aluminum scrap waste; aluminum hydroxide; ash containing precious 
  1672  metals or precious metal compounds; certain battery waste and scrap; 
  1673  certain semiconductor manufacturing equipment; certain pharmaceuticals 
  1674  and pharmaceutical ingredients; worked shell; worn clothing; and 
  1675  certain antiques, collectibles, and art.
  1676      With respect to certain animal products used as food for animals or 
  1677  an input in such food, commenters noted that these products are 
  1678  incorporated into U.S. animal nutrition programs that support 
  1679  livestock, poultry, aquaculture, and pet food production. According to 
  1680  commenters, there is little opportunity for import substitution for 
  1681  these products and any tariff applied to these products would impose 
  1682  additional costs on U.S. consumers.
  1683      With respect to seeds of a kind used for planting, commenters noted 
  1684  that tariffs on seeds have resulted in increased costs for U.S. seed 
  1685  producers and U.S. farmers. According to comments, tariffs that impact 
  1686  seed movement erode the ability of U.S. seed companies to provide U.S. 
  1687  farmers with pure, high-quality seeds at an affordable price due to the 
  1688  global nature of seed production. Specifically, many U.S. seed 
  1689  companies have foreign operations to take advantage of environmental 
  1690  and production conditions, such as additional growing seasons. 
  1691  Commenters also noted that the increased costs associated with seed 
  1692  production could reduce choices in the marketplace for consumers as 
  1693  certain varieties of seed will no longer be viable for 
  1694  commercialization in the United States.
  1695      With respect to certain vegetable products, commenters noted that 
  1696  certain products falling under the relevant HTSUS subheading are 
  1697  already included in Annex A to the June 5, 2026 FRN, but that the 
  1698  proposed product exemptions are limited to products used for religious 
  1699  purposes only. According to comments, products in the relevant HTSUS 
  1700  subheading are essential growing-media and fiber inputs used in nursery 
  1701  production that have no domestic source, including coconut coir, jute 
  1702  burlap, and sisal twine. According to comments, the crops used to 
  1703  produce these products are not commercially grown in the United States 
  1704  given climate limitations and, therefore, there is no domestic industry 
  1705  capable of producing these inputs for the U.S. horticulture sector.
  1706      With respect to in-quota imports of certain sugar and sugar-
  1707  containing products, commenters noted that U.S. sugar producers are 
  1708  more efficient than ever and domestic sugar yields have increased, yet 
  1709  the United States has never produced enough sugar to meet its domestic 
  1710  demand. To meet this demand, the United States has historically had to 
  1711  import significant amounts of sugar. According to comments, U.S. sugar 
  1712  processing
  1713  
  1714  [[Page 47332]]
  1715  
  1716  facilities rely on certain in-quota sugar to meet U.S. demand and 
  1717  supply a critical input of the U.S. food supply chain.
  1718      With respect to unflavored instant coffee, commenters noted that 
  1719  unflavored instant coffee is not available from domestic sources in 
  1720  sufficient quantities for U.S. consumers and coffee companies, 
  1721  including value-added manufacturers. These comments also maintained 
  1722  that over 99 percent of instant coffee imports come from economies 
  1723  covered by these investigations and there are not adequate non-tariffed 
  1724  alternatives. Commenters also noted that U.S. coffee companies will 
  1725  continue to be at a disadvantage producing and innovating ready-to-
  1726  drink and cold brew coffee compared to their foreign competitors if 
  1727  tariffs on unflavored instant coffee are imposed.
  1728      With respect to certain fertilizer inputs and pesticide inputs, 
  1729  commenters noted that imposing additional duties on these chemicals 
  1730  could cause disruptions or shortages in the domestic supply due to the 
  1731  limited availability of certain active ingredients outside of the 
  1732  investigated economies and because these products cannot be produced in 
  1733  the United States in sufficient quantities to meet domestic demand. 
  1734  Commenters also noted that the exemptions would be essential to avoid 
  1735  tariff inversion, causing U.S. manufacturers who produce value-added 
  1736  products to be disadvantaged in comparison to importers of finished 
  1737  agriculture chemical products.
  1738      With respect to certain animal hides and leather products, 
  1739  commenters noted that certain types of exotic leather--including 
  1740  reptile and ostrich--cannot be obtained in the United States because 
  1741  there is no domestic supply. According to commenters, tariffs would 
  1742  cause the migration of exotic leather manufacturing and American jobs 
  1743  to other countries, such as Mexico.
  1744      With respect to certain wood and wood products, commenters noted 
  1745  that certain types of wood and wood product imports--including 
  1746  eucalyptus and certain eucalyptus products--are not available from 
  1747  domestic producers in sufficient quantities to meet U.S. demand. 
  1748  According to commenters, these products are raw material inputs that 
  1749  are used to make timber and crane mats necessary in U.S. construction, 
  1750  powerline installation, and heavy civil infrastructure.
  1751      With respect to vanadium oxides and hydroxides, commenters noted 
  1752  that these products are necessary critical mineral inputs for which 
  1753  there is no or insufficient primary production in the United States and 
  1754  additional tariffs on these materials would cause serious supply

  2096  
  2097      For convenience and concision, this Notice has set out the actions 
  2098  of the Trade Representative in each of the 60 investigations of the 
  2099  acts, policies, and practices of each investigated economy related to 
  2100  its failure to enact and effectively enforce a forced labor import

  2102      The actions taken by the Trade Representative in this Notice with 
  2103  respect to the acts, policies, and practices of an economy in one 
  2104  investigation are separate from the actions taken with respect to the 
  2105  acts, policies, and practices of each other economy in other 
  2106  investigations by the Trade Representative. Each tariff action as to an 
  2107  economy in one investigation is separate from every other tariff action 
  2108  in other investigations and is for the distinct purpose of obtaining 
  2109  the elimination of the applicable economy's acts, policies, and 
  2110  practices found actionable under Section 301 in that investigation.

  2112  in this Notice in one investigation is only for the purpose of 
  2113  obtaining the elimination of the applicable economy's acts, policies, 
  2114  and practices found actionable under Section 301 in that investigation 
  2115  and not for any other purpose.
  2116      Each tariff action as to an economy taken by the Trade 
  2117  Representative in this Notice is intended to operate independently of 
  2118  each other, and the potential invalidity of one tariff action taken in 
  2119  this Notice should not affect any other tariff. The potential 
  2120  invalidity of one aspect of any tariff action taken in this Notice 
  2121  should not affect any other aspect of the tariff action.

  2123  taken by the Trade Representative in this Notice with respect to any 
  2124  Section 301 investigation to be invalid, only that tariff in that 
  2125  investigation should be treated as invalid, and any other tariff action 
  2126  taken in this Notice with respect to that investigation, or any other 
  2127  investigation, and the remainder of the actions in this Notice should 
  2128  continue to apply and should not be affected. Should a court hold that 
  2129  any aspect of any tariff action taken by the Trade Representative in 
  2130  this Notice with respect to any Section 301 investigation to be 
  2131  invalid, only that aspect of that tariff action should be treated as 
  2132  invalid.

  2134  this Notice is feasible and appropriate to obtain the elimination of 
  2135  the applicable economy's acts, policies, and practices the Trade 
  2136  Representative has found actionable under Section 301 in that 
  2137  investigation. If any aspect of the tariff action for an economy is 
  2138  held to be invalid, the remaining aspects of the tariff action and each 
  2139  tariff for a product of an investigated economy would remain 
  2140  appropriate and feasible to obtain the elimination of the applicable 
  2141  economy's acts, policies, or practices found actionable under Section 
  2142  301 in that investigation.
  2143      This section reflects the Trade Representative's intent that each 
  2144  tariff action and each exemption for a product of an investigated 
  2145  economy as set forth in section II.B of this Notice remain operative to

  2156  every tariff action and exemption in each investigation as set forth in 
  2157  this Notice is lawful. This section reflects the Trade Representative's 
  2158  view that each tariff action taken by the Trade Representative in this 
  2159  Notice should remain operative to obtain the elimination of the

  2161  under Section 301.

   286  IV. Proposed Actions To Be Taken in the Investigations
   287  
   288      Section 301(b) of the Trade Act provides that upon determining that 
   289  the acts, policies, and practices under investigation are actionable 
   290  and that action is appropriate, the Trade Representative shall take all 
   291  appropriate and feasible action authorized under section 301(c), 
   292  subject to the specific direction, if any, of the President regarding 
   293  such action, and all other appropriate and feasible action within the 
   294  power of the President, that the President may direct the Trade 
   295  Representative to take under section 301(b), to obtain the elimination 
   296  of that act, policy, or practice.
   297      Section 301(c) of the Trade Act authorizes the Trade Representative 
   298  to take certain actions for purposes of carrying out the provisions of 
   299  Section 301(b). Among others, Section 301(c)(1)(B) authorizes the Trade 
   300  Representative to ``impose duties or other import restrictions'' on the 
   301  goods of the foreign country subject to the investigation.
   302      Pursuant to Sections 301(b) and (c), the Trade Representative 
   303  proposes to determine that action is appropriate and that appropriate 
   304  action to obtain the elimination of the acts, policies, and practices 
   305  would include the imposition of ad valorem duties on all products of 
   306  the 60 economies subject to investigations, except as provided in Annex 
   307  A to this Notice. The proposed exemptions in Annex A include all 
   308  articles and parts currently subject to section 232 tariffs and raw 
   309  materials that if subject to the proposed additional tariffs could lead 
   310  to the unavailability of domestic supply. Annex A also includes 
   311  products that could cause economy-wide disruptions if subject to the 
   312  proposed additional tariffs and certain products that cannot be grown 
   313  or produced in sufficient quantities in the United States or obtained 
   314  from other sources. The proposed exemptions include informational 
   315  materials (e.g., books), donations, and accompanied baggage. Finally, 
   316  the proposed exemptions include articles for which additional tariffs 
   317  may not contribute substantially to the elimination of the investigated 
   318  acts, policies, and practices described above.
   319      For economies that impose a forced labor import prohibition--
   320  Canada, Ecuador, the European Union, Indonesia, Mexico, and Pakistan; 
   321  for economies that have undertaken commitments in their respective 
   322  Agreements on Reciprocal Trade regarding forced labor import 
   323  prohibitions--Argentina, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Ecuador, El Salvador, 
   324  Guatemala, Indonesia, Malaysia, and Taiwan; and economies that have 
   325  imposed a partial regime with the effect of preventing the importation 
   326  of certain forced labor goods--the United Kingdom; the Trade 
   327  Representative proposes additional duties of 10% for products of these 
   328  economies. For all other economies that have failed to impose and 
   329  effectively enforce a forced labor import prohibition, the Trade 
   330  Representative proposes 12.5% as the rate of additional duties.
   331      The Trade Representative also proposes a textile mechanism that 
   332  would allow for a certain volume of apparel and textile imports to 
   333  enter the United States at a reduced Section 301 tariff rate. Under 
   334  such a textile mechanism, the volume of reduced-duty imports from 
   335  certain trading partners would be equivalent to the quantity of exports 
   336  of textiles (e.g., U.S. produced man-made and cotton fiber textile 
   337  inputs) from the United States to that trading partner. A certain 
   338  volume of apparel and textile imports would also be allowed to enter 
   339  the United States at the reduced Section 301 rate based on the volume 
   340  of U.S. cotton and cotton products a trading partner imports from the 
   341  United States during a certain period of time.

   343  V. Response to Significant Comments
   344  
   345      USTR responds below to significant issues raised in the public 
   346  comments and hearings in response to the March 17, 2026, Federal 
   347  Register notice.
   348  
   349  Response to Significant Comments Raising Legal Arguments Regarding 
   350  Findings of ``Unreasonableness''
   351  
   352      Multiple comments raised threshold arguments that the Trade 
   353  Representative should not find that the failure of an economy to impose 
   354  and effectively enforce a prohibition on the importation of goods 
   355  produced with forced labor is unreasonable where: (1) an economy has 
   356  domestic laws prohibiting forced labor; (2) where no international 
   357  standards exists which provide an affirmative obligation on economies 
   358  to impose a forced labor import prohibition; or (3) where an economy 
   359  has otherwise made commitments to the United States with respect to 
   360  imposing and/or enforcing a forced labor import prohibition. This 
   361  section takes each of these arguments in turn.
   362      With respect to the first argument, and as explained in the Report 
   363  and above, solely prohibiting forced labor domestically is unreasonable 
   364  because it fails to discipline the influx of forced labor goods or to 
   365  prevent domestic producers from using forced labor inputs. Thus, while 
   366  an economy may have taken steps to ensure that the condition of forced 
   367  labor is extinguished within its borders, the economy nevertheless 
   368  permits market conditions where imported forced labor goods have a 
   369  competitive advantage over U.S. goods imported into their economy.
   370      In response to the second argument, USTR notes the Section 301 
   371  statute,
   372  
   373  [[Page 34275]]
   374  
   375  which governs these investigations, does not require the existence of 
   376  international standards discipling specific conduct as a prerequisite 
   377  to a finding of an unreasonable act, policy, or practice under Section 
   378  301(b) of the Trade Act. As explained in the Report, the definition of 
   379  unreasonable acts, policies, and practices in Section 301(d) 
   380  contemplates circumstances where, as here, acts, policies, and 
   381  practices of a foreign country may not be inconsistent with or violate 
   382  the international legal rights of the United States, but are 
   383  nevertheless unfair. Thus, the statutory structure of Section 301 
   384  contemplates that the Trade Representative may find unreasonable 
   385  conduct on the part of a trading partner even in the absence of 
   386  international standards or obligations.
   387      Third, some comments argued that where an economy has made 
   388  commitments to the United States regarding forced labor import 
   389  prohibitions, including through an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade, the 
   390  Trade Representative is without basis to find that same economy's 
   391  failure to impose and effectively enforce a forced labor import 
   392  prohibition is unreasonable. USTR applauds Argentina, Bangladesh, 
   393  Cambodia, Ecuador, El Salvador, Guatemala, Indonesia, Malaysia, and 
   394  Taiwan, which have undertaken commitments regarding a forced labor 
   395  import prohibition. However, commitments to take action in the future 
   396  is distinct from forbidding legally the importation of forced labor 
   397  goods, and effectively enforcing such prohibition. Until such time as 
   398  the commitment is implemented, U.S. products will continue to compete 
   399  against forced labor products that have a competitive advantage in 
   400  global markets which, among other reasons explained in the Report, is 
   401  unreasonable.
   402      The Trade Representative fully expects economies that have 
   403  undertaken commitments related to prohibiting the importation of forced 
   404  labor goods to abide by those commitments. Accordingly, the Trade 
   405  Representative proposes that the additional duty rate to be applied in 
   406  the investigations take into account whether an economy has undertaken 
   407  such commitments.

   409  Response to Significant Comments Regarding Actions To Be Taken in the 
   410  Investigations
   411  
   412      A number of comments responded on potential responsive action by 
   413  the Trade Representative. These comments recommended that the Trade 
   414  Representative engage in multilateral negotiations, including at the 
   415  ILO, to encourage economies to impose a forced labor import prohibition 
   416  rather than take ``punitive measures,'' and to provide capacity 
   417  building and technical assistance, especially to developing economies, 
   418  to encourage effective enforcement of such a prohibition.
   419      The Trade Representative proposes that taking an action is 
   420  appropriate, and that action includes the imposition of additional 
   421  duties on products of the investigated economies, in order to obtain

   423  However, the Trade Representative will continue to consider these

tools.name: fr_search

query.description: Full-text search terms; "" for none. Supports quoted phrases, e.g. "\"extension of stay\" F-1".
query.title: Query

doc_type.description: Document types: RULE, PRORULE (proposed rule), NOTICE, PRESDOCU (presidential document). null for all.
doc_type.title: Doc Type

agency.description: Agency slugs, e.g. homeland-security-department, u-s-citizenship-and-immigration-services, u-s-immigration-and-customs-enforcement, state-department, labor-department, executive-office-of-the-president.
agency.title: Agency

pres_type.description: Presidential document subtypes (use with doc_type PRESDOCU).
pres_type.title: Pres Type

cfr.description: CFR title:part affected, e.g. 8:214. The part must be numeric; lettered parts are not supported by this filter.
cfr.title: Cfr

tools.description: Search U.S. Federal Register documents (rules, proposed rules, notices, presidential documents) by keywords and filters. Prints document numbers, titles, types, dates, citations, dockets, RINs and abstracts.

tools.name: fr_doc
tools.description: Metadata for one Federal Register document: title, type, action, citation, page range, publication/signing/effective dates, comment deadline, docket, RIN, CFR parts affected, corrections, abstract.

tools.name: fr_toc
tools.description: Outline of a document's full text: headings with line numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_grep

pattern.description: Python regular expression, searched over the whole text (a match may span lines). ^ and $ match at line boundaries; . does not match a newline.
pattern.title: Pattern

context.description: Lines of context around each match (default 2, at most 10).
context.title: Context

tools.description: Regex search inside one document's full text. Shows the lines of each match with line numbers, context lines and the FR page of each match. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_text
tools.description: Read a document's full text by line range, with line numbers. [[Page N]] markers give FR page numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

answer.description: Direct answer to each lettered part, in order, labelled (a), (b), ...
answer.title: Answer

basis.description: Provisions and documents relied on, with citations.
basis.title: Basis

uncertainty.description: What the documents leave open, or "None".
uncertainty.title: Uncertainty

    38  the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement, for purposes of implementing 
    39  tariffs pursuant to Proclamation 11032 of June 1, 2026.
    40  
    41  DATES: The guidance set out in in this notice is effective with respect 
    42  to products that are entered for consumption, or withdrawn from 
    43  warehouse for consumption, on or after 12:01 a.m. Eastern Time on 
    44  October 14, 2026.
    45  
    46  SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
    47  
    48  Background
    49  
    50      On June 1, 2026, the President issued Presidential Proclamation 
    51  11032 entitled ``Further Adjusting the Tariff Regimes for Imports of 
    52  Aluminum, Steel, and Copper into the United States'' (91 FR 34085) 
    53  (Proclamation). The Proclamation modifies the tariff regimes for metal 
    54  products imposed in Presidential Proclamation 9704, as amended, 
    55  Proclamation 9705, as amended, and Proclamation 10962, as amended, and 
    56  directs the Secretary of Commerce (Secretary) to issue guidance to U.S. 
    57  Customs and Border Protection regarding the assessment of ``U.S. 
    58  content'' for purposes of implementing tariffs pursuant to clause 
    59  (2)(d) of the Proclamation. The Secretary has delegated this duty to 
    60  the Deputy Assistant Secretary for Technology Security.
    61  
    62  Guidance to U.S. Customs and Border Protection Regarding the Assessment 
    63  of ``U.S. Content'' for Purposes of Implementing Tariffs Pursuant to 
    64  Clause (2)(d) of Proclamation 11032 of June 1, 2026
    65  
    66      The Department of Commerce advises that, for purposes of 
    67  implementing clause (2)(d) of the Proclamation, the term ``U.S. 
    68  content'' means the following:
    69      1. The value of the product attributable to parts wholly obtained, 
    70  entirely produced, or substantially transformed in the United States, 
    71  and
    72      2. To the extent not otherwise accounted for in (1), the value of 
    73  the product attributable to steel that was melted and poured in the 
    74  United States, aluminum that was smelted and cast in the United States, 
    75  and/or copper that was smelted and cast in the United States.
    76      Questions regarding the application of this Notice to a specific 
    77  product may be directed to U.S. Customs and Border Protection.
    78

    38                  Section 1. Purpose. The United States has imposed 
    39                  tariffs under various statutory authorities and through 
    40                  a number of Executive Orders and proclamations to 
    41                  protect national security and address unusual and 
    42                  extraordinary threats to the national security, foreign 
    43                  policy, and economy of the United States. Although each 
    44                  of these actions, as listed in section 2 of this order, 
    45                  serves separate and distinct policy purposes, I have 
    46                  now determined that, to the extent these tariffs apply 
    47                  to the same article, these tariffs should not all have 
    48                  a cumulative effect (or ``stack'' on top of one 
    49                  another) because the rate of duty resulting from such 
    50                  stacking exceeds what is necessary to achieve the 
    51                  intended policy goals. To avoid the cumulative effect 
    52                  of overlapping tariffs on certain articles, this order 
    53                  sets out the procedure for determining which of 
    54                  multiple tariffs shall apply to an article when that 
    55                  article is subject to more than one of the actions 
    56                  listed in section 2 of this order.
    57  
    58                  Sec. 2. Applicability. This order shall apply only to 
    59                  the administration of tariffs imposed through the 
    60                  following actions and subsequent amendments to those 
    61                  tariffs:

    64                  Imports of Automobiles and Automobile Parts Into the 
    65                  United States);

    69                  Order 14197 of February 3, 2025 (Progress on the

    80                  Southern Border), Executive Order 14227 of March 2, 
    81                  2025 (Amendment to Duties To Address the Situation at 
    82                  Our Southern Border), and Executive Order 14232 of

    84                  of Illicit Drugs Across Our Southern Border);

    86                  Imports of Aluminum Into the United States), as amended

    91                  Imports of Aluminum Into the United States); and
    92                      (e) Proclamation 9705 of March 8, 2018 (Adjusting 
    93                  Imports of Steel Into the United States), as amended by 
    94                  Proclamation 9980 of January 24, 2020 (Adjusting 
    95                  Imports of Derivative Aluminum Articles and Derivative 
    96                  Steel
    97  
    98  [[Page 18908]]
    99  
   100                  Articles Into the United States), and Proclamation 
   101                  10896 of February 10, 2025 (Adjusting Imports of Steel 
   102                  Into the United States).
   103  
   104                  Sec. 3. Non-Stacking of Tariff Measures. (a) 
   105                  Notwithstanding any provision of any action listed in 
   106                  section 2 of this order, tariffs for articles subject 
   107                  to tariffs under the actions listed in section 2 of 
   108                  this order shall apply as follows:
   109  
   110  (i) An article subject to tariffs pursuant to the action listed in section 
   111  (2)(a) of this order shall not be subject to additional tariffs on that 
   112  article pursuant to the actions listed in sections 2(b) through 2(e) of 
   113  this order.
   114  
   115  (ii) An article subject to tariffs pursuant to the actions listed in 
   116  section 2(b) or 2(c) of this order shall not be subject to additional 
   117  tariffs on that article pursuant to the actions listed in section 2(d) or 
   118  2(e) of this order.

   140                  tariff imposed pursuant to subsection (a) of this 
   141                  section and one or more tariffs imposed pursuant to an

   143                  order, then the tariff imposed on the article pursuant 
   144                  to subsection (a) of this section shall be cumulative 
   145                  with the tariff or tariffs imposed pursuant to the 
   146                  action or actions not listed in section 2 of this 
   147                  order.

   150                  Nothing in this order shall be interpreted to alter or 
   151                  limit the application of any duties, taxes, fees, or 
   152                  exactions other than those imposed pursuant to the

   161                  (HTSUS); duties imposed pursuant to section 301 of the 
   162                  Trade Act of 1974, as amended; duties imposed pursuant 
   163                  to Executive Order 14195 of February 1, 2025 (Imposing 
   164                  Duties To Address the Synthetic Opioid Supply Chain in 
   165                  the People's Republic of China), as amended; and 
   166                  antidumping and countervailing duties.

   169                  Security, acting through the Commissioner of U.S. 
   170                  Customs and Border Protection and in consultation with 
   171                  the Secretary of the Treasury, shall take all necessary 
   172                  steps to update guidance, systems, and enforcement 
   173                  mechanisms, including to revise, suspend, or rescind 
   174                  any regulations that may be inconsistent with this 
   175                  order, to reflect the policy set forth in this order.
   176  
   177                      (b) The Secretary of Commerce and the Secretary of 
   178                  Homeland Security, in coordination with the Secretary 
   179                  of the Treasury and the United States Trade 
   180                  Representative, shall provide additional guidance as 
   181                  necessary to ensure consistent interpretation and 
   182                  application of the policy set forth in this order.

   184                  authorized to determine whether changes to the HTSUS

   187  [[Page 18909]]
   188  
   189                  of the United States International Trade Commission to

    27  -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    28  
    29  SUMMARY: In order to effectuate the President's Executive Order 14289, 
    30  ``Addressing Certain Tariffs on Imported Articles,'' which eliminates 
    31  the compounding or ``stacking'' of certain overlapping tariffs that 
    32  were imposed under various statutory authorities and Executive orders 
    33  to protect national security and address unusual and extraordinary 
    34  threats to the national security, foreign policy, and economy of the 
    35  United States, the Secretary of Homeland Security has determined that 
    36  appropriate action is needed to ensure collection of applicable duties 
    37  as well as to modify the Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the United 
    38  States (HTSUS) as set out in the Annex to this notice.
    39  
    40  DATES: The HTSUS is modified with respect to covered articles, as set 
    41  out in the Annex to this document, at 12:01 a.m. eastern daylight time 
    42  on May 16, 2025. The amendments shall apply to all covered articles 
    43  that were entered for consumption, or withdrawn from warehouse for 
    44  consumption, as specified in the Annex to this document. Requests for 
    45  refunds may be filed on or after May 16, 2025.
    46

    48  Trade Policy and Programs, Office of Trade, U.S. Customs and Border 
    49  Protection, (202) 325-6432 or by email at [email protected]. C. 
    50  Shane Campbell, Acting Executive Director, Cargo and Conveyance 
    51  Security, Office of Field Operations, U.S. Customs and Border 
    52  Protection, (202) 344-3401 or by email at [email protected].
    53  
    54  SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: The United States has imposed tariffs under 
    55  various statutory authorities, including the International Emergency 
    56  Economic Powers Act (50 U.S.C. 1701 et seq.) (IEEPA), the National 
    57  Emergencies Act (50 U.S.C. 1601 et seq.), section 604 of the Trade Act 
    58  of 1974, as amended (19 U.S.C. 2483), section 232 of the Trade 
    59  Expansion Act of 1962, as amended (19 U.S.C. 1862), section 301 of 
    60  title 3, United States Code, and Executive orders to protect national 
    61  security, confront unusual and extraordinary threats to the national 
    62  security, foreign policy, and economy of the United States, and promote 
    63  the interests of American workers and industries. Although many of 
    64  these actions, as listed below, serve separate and distinct policy 
    65  purposes, on April 29, 2025, the President issued Executive Order 
    66  14289, ``Addressing Certain Tariffs on Imported Articles'' (90 FR 
    67  18907), in which the President determined that these tariffs should not 
    68  all have a cumulative effect (or ``stack'' on top of one another). 
    69  Therefore, to avoid the cumulative effect of overlapping tariffs on 
    70  certain articles, Executive Order 14289 sets forth procedures for 
    71  determining which tariffs should apply to an article when that article 
    72  is subject to more than one of the actions listed in section 2 of 
    73  Executive Order 14289, and set forth here:
    74      (a) Proclamation 10908 of March 26, 2025 (``Adjusting Imports of 
    75  Automobiles and Automobile Parts Into the United States'');
    76      (b) Executive Order 14193 of February 1, 2025 (``Imposing Duties To 
    77  Address the Flow of Illicit Drugs Across Our Northern Border''), as 
    78  amended by Executive Order 14197 of February 3, 2025 (``Progress on the 
    79  Situation at Our Northern Border''), Executive Order 14226 of March 2, 
    80  2025 (``Amendment to Duties To Address the Flow of Illicit Drugs Across 
    81  Our Northern Border''), and Executive Order 14231 of March 6, 2025

    84      (c) Executive Order 14194 of February 1, 2025 (``Imposing Duties To 
    85  Address the Situation at Our Southern Border''), as amended by 
    86  Executive Order 14198 of February 3, 2025 (``Progress on the Situation 
    87  at Our Southern Border''), Executive Order 14227 of March 2, 2025 
    88  (``Amendment to Duties To Address the Situation at Our Southern 
    89  Border''), and Executive Order 14232 of March 6, 2025 (``Amendment to 
    90  Duties to Address the Flow of Illicit Drugs Across Our Southern 
    91  Border'');
    92      (d) Proclamation 9704 of March 8, 2018 (``Adjusting Imports of 
    93  Aluminum Into the United States''),\1\ as amended by Proclamation 9980 
    94  of January 24, 2020 (``Adjusting Imports of Derivative Aluminum 
    95  Articles and Derivative Steel Articles Into the United States''), and 
    96  Proclamation 10895 of February 10, 2025 (``Adjusting Imports of 
    97  Aluminum Into the United States'');

   157  States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA), will not be subject to

    88      Title: Court-Ordered Refunds under the International Emergency 
    89  Economic Powers Act Worksheet.
    90      OMB Number: 1651-0149.
    91      Form Number: N/A.
    92      Current Actions: Extension.
    93      Type of Review: Extension.
    94      Affected Public: Businesses.
    95      Abstract:
    96  
    97  Background
    98  
    99      On February 20, 2026, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled in Learning 
   100  Resources, Inc. v. Trump that all tariffs imposed by the President 
   101  under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA), which 
   102  U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) has collected pursuant to the 
   103  President's Executive Orders and associated provisions in the 
   104  Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the United States (HTSUS) since February 
   105  3, 2025, were unlawful. In so holding, the Supreme Court affirmed the 
   106  August 29, 2025 judgment of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal 
   107  Circuit (CAFC) in V.O.S. Selections, Inc. v. Trump, which in turn had 
   108  affirmed-in-part, vacated-in-part, and remanded-in-part the May 28, 
   109  2025 decision of the U.S. Court of International Trade (CIT) in that 
   110  case. On March 2, 2026, the CAFC issued its formal mandate to the CIT.
   111      On March 4, 2026, the CIT ordered in Atmus Filtration, Inc. v. 
   112  United States ``that, with respect to any and all unliquidated entries 
   113  that were entered subject to the IEEPA duties, U.S. Customs and Border 
   114  Protection is hereby directed to liquidate those entries without regard 
   115  to the IEEPA duties,'' and ``[a]ny liquidated entries for which 
   116  liquidation is not final shall be reliquidated without regard to IEEPA 
   117  duties.'' On March 5, 2026, the CIT amended its March 4, 2026, order in 
   118  Atmus Filtration, Inc. v. United States to clarify that it applies to 
   119  entries made ``subject to the IEEPA duties imposed by the Executive 
   120  Orders considered by the Supreme Court in Learning Resources, Inc. v. 
   121  Trump.'' On March 6, 2026, the CIT suspended its March 4, 2026, order, 
   122  as amended, ``to the extent that it directs immediate compliance,'' to 
   123  allow CBP time to develop an automated tool capable of processing the 
   124  unprecedented volume and value of refunds covered by the CIT order. On 
   125  the same day, the CIT also ordered the government to provide periodic 
   126  status reporting on this development. The government submitted detailed 
   127  status reports to the court on March 12, 2026, and March 19, 2026.
   128      On March 20, 2026, the CIT again amended its Amended Order of March 
   129  5, 2026, to clarify that it applies to ``any and all unliquidated 
   130  entries that were entered subject to IEEPA duties'' as well as to any 
   131  such ``liquidated entries for which liquidation is not final,'' 
   132  provided, however, that ``nothing in this order addresses issues 
   133  concerning duty free de minimis treatment under 19 U.S.C. 1321 that are 
   134  otherwise before this Court'' in Axle of Dearborn, Inc. v. Department 
   135  of Commerce. The CIT's March 20, 2026 order continued to suspend the 
   136  Amended Order of March 5, 2026, ``to the extent that it requires 
   137  immediate compliance,'' and ordered that the government file another 
   138  status report on March 31, 2026, ``describing the progress Customs has 
   139  made toward the completion of a process to issue refunds of IEEPA 
   140  duties paid with interest,'' and join another closed settlement 
   141  conference with the Court later the same day to further discuss the 
   142  same. In accordance with this order, the government submitted a 
   143  detailed status report and attended a closed settlement conference on 
   144  March 31, 2026. On April 6, 2026, the plaintiff in Atmus Filtration, 
   145  Inc. v. United States filed a notice of voluntary dismissal in its 
   146  case, which the CIT granted on April 8, 2026.
   147      On April 7, 2026, the CIT lifted the stay on Euro-Notions Florida, 
   148  Inc. v. United States, CIT Ct. No. 25-00595, another pending case 
   149  challenging the IEEPA duties, and issued an injunctive order 
   150  substantively identical to its March 4, 2026, order, as amended, in 
   151  Atmus Filtration, Inc. Accordingly, the Euro-Notions Florida, Inc. case 
   152  has replaced the Atmus Filtration, Inc. case as the test case for the 
   153  IEEPA refund process. On April 8, 2026, the CIT issued an order in 
   154  Euro-Notions Florida, Inc. ordering the government to file another 
   155  status update on April 14, 2026, regarding CBP's progress on the IEEPA 
   156  duty refund process and join another closed settlement conference with 
   157  the Court later the same day.
   158      Specifically, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and CBP 
   159  have initiated the development of the Consolidated Administration and 
   160  Processing of Entries (CAPE) tool to handle the volume of tariff 
   161  refunds anticipated in the timeframe required by the CIT. While the CIT 
   162  has not set a timeframe to date, the Court has signaled that refunds be 
   163  issued as quickly as possible because of the accrual of interest. 
   164  Further, while the order to refund IEEPA duties with interest is 
   165  currently suspended ``to the extent that it requires immediate 
   166  compliance,'' the CIT is closely monitoring CBP's progress to timely 
   167  complete the development of CAPE and can lift the suspension of its 
   168  order at any time.
   169      The tariffs assessed under IEEPA from February 3, 2025 to February 
   170  24, 2026 total an estimated $166 billion, with over 53 million entry 
   171  summaries requiring processing in order to issue accurate refunds with 
   172  required interest. Prior to CAPE, refunds were reviewed and processed 
   173  entry summary-by-entry summary. Given the volume and values of the 
   174  entries affected by the CIT order, CBP is unable to process the refunds 
   175  owed in a timely or efficient manner using the existing process.
   176      The CAPE tool may be accessed through CBP's Automated Commercial 
   177  Environment (ACE), which is the CBP-operated system used to report, 
   178  manage, process, and track U.S. imports and exports.
   179      The CAPE tool allows CBP to process multiple entry summaries by the 
   180  same importer on a single submission, which will lead to a single 
   181  refund for a given importer rather than multiple refund transactions. 
   182  Importers are able to file as many CAPE Declarations as they need. 
   183  Thus, potentially thousands of refund transactions can be consolidated 
   184  into a single payment that is directly deposited into an IOR's account 
   185  (or the account of their designated party) on file. The request for a 
   186  refund that is filed through CAPE is called a ``CAPE Declaration''.
   187      The new CAPE tool allows--
   188       Automated processes to be leveraged to the fullest extent 
   189  possible to segment risk and execute millions of mathematical 
   190  calculations with precision.
   191       CBP personnel to focus on those refund CAPE Declarations 
   192  that are considered ``high risk'' due to the dollar values involved or 
   193  the risk profile of the IOR.
   194       CBP personnel to determine with confidence which lines on 
   195  an entry summary are eligible for an IEEPA refund while ensuring the 
   196  remaining duties (including duties owed for antidumping/countervailing 
   197  duty (AD/CVD) remedies and Section 232 tariffs), tax, and fees that are 
   198  owed the U.S. government are retained and collected as usual.
   199       CBP personnel to ensure that the precise duty owed to the 
   200  IOR is refunded directly to the IOR's account--

   172  entry summary-by-entry summary. Given the volume and values of the 
   173  entries affected by the CIT order, CBP is unable to process the refunds 
   174  owed in a timely or efficient manner using the existing process.
   175      The CAPE tool may be accessed through CBP's Automated Commercial 
   176  Environment (ACE), which is the CBP-operated system used to report, 
   177  manage, process, and track U.S. imports and exports.
   178      The CAPE tool allows CBP to process multiple entry summaries by the 
   179  same importer on a single submission, which will lead to a single 
   180  refund for a given importer rather than multiple refund transactions. 
   181  Importers are able to file as many CAPE Declarations as they need. 
   182  Thus, potentially thousands of refund transactions can be consolidated 
   183  into a single payment that is directly deposited into an IOR's account 
   184  (or the account of their designated party) on file. The request for a 
   185  refund that is filed through CAPE is called a ``CAPE Declaration''.
   186      The new CAPE tool allows--
   187       Automated processes to be leveraged to the fullest extent 
   188  possible to segment risk and execute millions of mathematical 
   189  calculations with precision.
   190       CBP personnel to focus on those refund CAPE Declarations 
   191  that are considered ``high risk'' due to the dollar values involved or 
   192  the risk profile of the IOR.
   193       CBP personnel to determine with confidence which lines on 
   194  an entry summary are eligible for an IEEPA refund while ensuring the 
   195  remaining duties (including duties owed for antidumping/countervailing 
   196  duty (AD/CVD) remedies and Section 232 tariffs), tax, and fees that are 
   197  owed the U.S. government are retained and collected as usual.
   198       CBP personnel to ensure that the precise duty owed to the 
   199  IOR is refunded directly to the IOR's account--no overpayments or 
   200  payments to an erroneous party.
