    28  
    29                  
    30  Imposing Duties To Address the Flow of Illicit 
    31                  Drugs Across Our Northern Border
    32  
    33                  By the authority vested in me as President by the 
    34                  Constitution and the laws of the United States of 
    35                  America, including the International Emergency Economic 
    36                  Powers Act (50 U.S.C. 1701 et seq.) (IEEPA), the 
    37                  National Emergencies Act (50 U.S.C. 1601 et seq.) 
    38                  (NEA), section 604 of the Trade Act of 1974, as amended 
    39                  (19 U.S.C. 2483), and section 301 of title 3, United 
    40                  States Code,
    41  
    42                  I, DONALD J. TRUMP, President of the United States of 
    43                  America, find that the sustained influx of illicit 
    44                  opioids and other drugs has profound consequences on 
    45                  our Nation, endangering lives and putting a severe 
    46                  strain on our healthcare system, public services, and 
    47                  communities.
    48  
    49                  This challenge threatens the fabric of our society. 
    50                  Gang members, smugglers, human traffickers, and illicit 
    51                  drugs of all kinds have poured across our borders and 
    52                  into our communities. Canada has played a central role 
    53                  in these challenges, including by failing to devote 
    54                  sufficient attention and resources or meaningfully 
    55                  coordinate with United States law enforcement partners 
    56                  to effectively stem the tide of illicit drugs.
    57  
    58                  Drug trafficking organizations (DTOs) are the world's 
    59                  leading producers of fentanyl, methamphetamine, 
    60                  cocaine, and other illicit drugs, and they cultivate, 
    61                  process, and distribute massive quantities of narcotics 
    62                  that fuel addiction and violence in communities across 
    63                  the United States. These DTOs often collaborate with 
    64                  transnational cartels to smuggle illicit drugs into the 
    65                  United States, utilizing clandestine airstrips, 
    66                  maritime routes, and overland corridors.
    67  
    68                  The challenges at our southern border are foremost in 
    69                  the public consciousness, but our northern border is 
    70                  not exempt from these issues. Criminal networks are 
    71                  implicated in human trafficking and smuggling 
    72                  operations, enabling unvetted illegal migration across 
    73                  our northern border. There is also a growing presence 
    74                  of Mexican cartels operating fentanyl and nitazene 
    75                  synthesis labs in Canada. The flow of illicit drugs 
    76                  like fentanyl to the United States through both illicit 
    77                  distribution networks and international mail--due, in 
    78                  the case of the latter, to the existing administrative 
    79                  exemption from duty and taxes, also known as de 
    80                  minimis, under section 1321 of title 19, United States 
    81                  Code--has created a public health crisis in the United 
    82                  States, as outlined in the Presidential Memorandum of 
    83                  January 20, 2025 (America First Trade Policy) and 
    84                  Executive Order 14157 of January 20, 2025 (Designating 
    85                  Cartels and Other Organizations as Foreign Terrorist 
    86                  Organizations and Specially Designated Global 
    87                  Terrorists). With respect to smuggling of illicit drugs 
    88                  across our northern border, Canada's Financial 
    89                  Transactions and Reports Analysis Centre recently 
    90                  published a study on the laundering of proceeds of 
    91                  illicit synthetic opioids, which recognized Canada's 
    92                  heightened domestic production of fentanyl, largely 
    93                  from British Columbia, and its growing footprint within 
    94                  international narcotics distribution. Despite a North 
    95                  American dialogue on the public health impacts of 
    96                  illicit drugs since 2016, Canadian officials have 
    97                  acknowledged that the problem has only grown. And while 
    98                  U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) within the 
    99                  Department of Homeland Security seized, comparatively, 
   100                  much less fentanyl from Canada than from Mexico last 
   101                  year, fentanyl is so potent that even a very small 
   102                  parcel of the drug can cause many deaths and
   103  
   104  [[Page 9114]]
   105  
   106                  destruction to America families. In fact, the amount of 
   107                  fentanyl that crossed the northern border last year 
   108                  could kill 9.5 million Americans.
   109  
   110                  Immediate action is required to finally end this public 
   111                  health crisis and national emergency, which will not 
   112                  happen unless the compliance and cooperation of Canada 
   113                  is assured.
   114  
   115                  I hereby determine and order:
   116  
   117                  Section 1. (a) As President of the United States, my 
   118                  highest duty is the defense of the country and its 
   119                  citizens. A Nation without borders is not a nation at 
   120                  all. I will not stand by and allow our sovereignty to 
   121                  be eroded, our laws to be trampled, our citizens to be 
   122                  endangered, or our borders to be disrespected anymore.
   123  
   124                  I previously declared a national emergency with respect 
   125                  to the grave threat to the United States posed by the 
   126                  influx of illegal aliens and illicit drugs into the 
   127                  United States in Proclamation 10886 of January 20, 2025 
   128                  (Declaring a National Emergency at the Southern 
   129                  Border). Pursuant to the NEA, I hereby expand the scope 
   130                  of the national emergency declared in that Proclamation 
   131                  to cover the threat to the safety and security of 
   132                  Americans, including the public health crisis of deaths 
   133                  due to the use of fentanyl and other illicit drugs, and 
   134                  the failure of Canada to do more to arrest, seize, 
   135                  detain, or otherwise intercept DTOs, other drug and 
   136                  human traffickers, criminals at large, and drugs. In 
   137                  addition, this failure to act on the part of Canada 
   138                  constitutes an unusual and extraordinary threat, which 
   139                  has its source in substantial part outside the United 
   140                  States, to the national security and foreign policy of 
   141                  the United States. I hereby declare and reiterate a 
   142                  national emergency under the NEA and IEEPA to deal with 
   143                  that threat. This national emergency requires decisive 
   144                  and immediate action, and I have decided to impose, 
   145                  consistent with law, ad valorem tariffs on articles 
   146                  that are products of Canada set forth in this order. In 
   147                  doing so, I invoke my authority under section 
   148                  1702(a)(1)(B) of IEEPA, and specifically find that 
   149                  action under other authority to impose tariffs is 
   150                  inadequate to address this unusual and extraordinary 
   151                  threat.
   152  
   153                  Sec. 2. (a) All articles that are products of Canada as 
   154                  defined by the Federal Register notice described in 
   155                  subsection (e) of this section (Federal Register 
   156                  notice), and except for those products described in 
   157                  subsection (b) of this section, shall be, consistent 
   158                  with law, subject to an additional 25 percent ad 
   159                  valorem rate of duty. Such rate of duty shall apply 
   160                  with respect to goods entered for consumption, or 
   161                  withdrawn from warehouse for consumption, on or after 
   162                  12:01 a.m. eastern time on February 4, 2025, except 
   163                  that goods entered for consumption, or withdrawn from 
   164                  warehouse for consumption, after such time that were 
   165                  loaded onto a vessel at the port of loading or in 
   166                  transit on the final mode of transport prior to entry 
   167                  into the United States before 12:01 a.m. eastern time 
   168                  on February 1, 2025, shall not be subject to such 
   169                  additional duty, only if the importer certifies to CBP 
   170                  as specified in the Federal Register notice.
   171  
   172                      (b) With respect to energy or energy resources, as 
   173                  defined in section 8 of Executive Order 14156 of 
   174                  January 20, 2025 (Declaring a National Energy 
   175                  Emergency), and as otherwise included in the Federal 
   176                  Register notice, such articles that are products of 
   177                  Canada as defined by the Federal Register notice shall 
   178                  be, consistent with law, subject to an additional 10 
   179                  percent ad valorem rate of duty. Such rate of duty 
   180                  shall apply with respect to goods entered for 
   181                  consumption, or withdrawn from warehouse for 
   182                  consumption, on or after 12:01 a.m. eastern time on 
   183                  February 4, 2025, except that goods entered for 
   184                  consumption, or withdrawn from warehouse for 
   185                  consumption, after such time that were loaded onto a 
   186                  vessel at the port of loading or in transit on the 
   187                  final mode of transport prior to entry into the United 
   188                  States before 12:01 a.m. eastern time on February 1, 
   189                  2025, shall not be subject to such additional duty, 
   190                  only if the importer certifies to CBP as specified in 
   191                  the Federal Register notice.
   192                      (c) The rates of duty established by this order are 
   193                  in addition to any other duties, fees, exactions, or 
   194                  charges applicable to such imported articles.
   195  
   196  [[Page 9115]]
   197  
   198                      (d) Should Canada retaliate against the United 
   199                  States in response to this action through import duties 
   200                  on United States exports to Canada or similar measures, 
   201                  the President may increase or expand in scope the 
   202                  duties imposed under this order to ensure the efficacy 
   203                  of this action.
   204                      (e) In order to establish the duty rate on imports 
   205                  of articles that are products of Canada, the Secretary 
   206                  of Homeland Security shall determine the modifications 
   207                  necessary to the Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the 
   208                  United States (HTSUS) in order to effectuate this order 
   209                  consistent with law and shall make such modifications 
   210                  to the HTSUS through notice in the Federal Register. 
   211                  The modifications made to the HTSUS by this notice 
   212                  shall be effective with respect to goods entered for 
   213                  consumption, or withdrawn from warehouse for 
   214                  consumption, on or after 12:01 a.m. eastern time on 
   215                  February 4, 2025, and shall continue in effect until 
   216                  such actions are expressly reduced, modified, or 
   217                  terminated.
   218                      (f) Articles that are products of Canada, except 
   219                  those that are eligible for admission under ``domestic 
   220                  status'' as defined in 19 CFR 146.43, which are subject 
   221                  to the duties imposed by this order and are admitted 
   222                  into a United States foreign trade zone on or after 
   223                  12:01 a.m. eastern time on February 4, 2025, except as 
   224                  otherwise noted in subsections (a) and (b) of this 
   225                  section, must be admitted as ``privileged foreign 
   226                  status'' as defined in 19 CFR 146.41. Such articles 
   227                  will be subject upon entry for consumption to the rates 
   228                  of duty related to the classification under the 
   229                  applicable HTSUS subheading in effect at the time of 
   230                  admittance into the United States foreign trade zone.

    71                  By the authority vested in me as President by the

    80                  Section 1. Background. In Executive Order 14193 of

    68                  States
    69  
    70                  By the President of the United States of America
    71  
    72                  A Proclamation
    73  
    74                  1. On January 19, 2018, the Secretary of Commerce 
    75                  (Secretary) transmitted to me a report on his 
    76                  investigation into the effect of imports of aluminum on 
    77                  the national security of the United States under 
    78                  section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962, as 
    79                  amended (19 U.S.C. 1862) (section 232). The Secretary 
    80                  found and advised me of the Secretary's opinion that 
    81                  aluminum is being imported into the United States in 
    82                  such quantities and under such circumstances as to 
    83                  threaten to impair the national security of the United 
    84                  States.
    85  
    86                  2. In Proclamation 9704 of March 8, 2018 (Adjusting 
    87                  Imports of Aluminum Into the United States), I 
    88                  concurred in the Secretary's finding that aluminum was 
    89                  being imported into the United States in such 
    90                  quantities and under such circumstances as to threaten 
    91                  to impair the national security of the United States, 
    92                  and decided to adjust the imports of aluminum articles 
    93                  by imposing a 10 percent ad valorem tariff on such 
    94                  articles imported from most countries. Proclamation 
    95                  9704 further stated that any country with which the 
    96                  United States has a security relationship is welcome to 
    97                  discuss alternative ways to address the threatened 
    98                  impairment of the national security caused by imports 
    99                  from that country, and noted that, should the United 
   100                  States and any such country arrive at a satisfactory 
   101                  alternative means to address the threat to the national 
   102                  security such that I determine that imports from that 
   103                  country no longer threaten to impair the national 
   104                  security, I may remove or modify the restriction on 
   105                  aluminum articles imports from that country and, if 
   106                  necessary, adjust the tariff as it applies to other 
   107                  countries, as the national security interests of the 
   108                  United States require.
   109  
   110                  3. In Proclamation 9704, I also directed the Secretary 
   111                  to monitor imports of aluminum articles and inform me 
   112                  of any circumstances that in the Secretary's opinion 
   113                  might indicate the need for further action under 
   114                  section 232 with respect to such imports. Pursuant to 
   115                  Proclamation 9704, the Secretary was authorized to 
   116                  provide relief from the additional duties, based on a 
   117                  request from a directly affected party located in the 
   118                  United States, for any aluminum article determined not 
   119                  to be produced in the United States in a sufficient and 
   120                  reasonably available amount or of a satisfactory 
   121                  quality, or based upon specific national security 
   122                  considerations. Proclamation 9776 of August 29, 2018, 
   123                  and Proclamation 9980 of January 24, 2020, similarly 
   124                  authorized the Secretary to provide relief from certain 
   125                  tariffs on other aluminum products and derivatives set 
   126                  forth in those proclamations.
   127  
   128                  4. In subsequent proclamations, the President adjusted 
   129                  the tariffs applicable to aluminum articles imports 
   130                  from Argentina, Australia, Canada, Mexico, the European 
   131                  Union (EU), and the United Kingdom (UK), after engaging 
   132                  in discussions with each of those parties on 
   133                  alternative ways to address the threat to the national 
   134                  security from such imports.
   135  
   136                  5. The Secretary has informed me that, notwithstanding 
   137                  the 10 percent ad valorem tariff imposed by 
   138                  Proclamation 9704 that mitigated the threatened 
   139                  impairment of our national security, aluminum imports 
   140                  into the United States have continued at unacceptable 
   141                  levels as the global aluminum excess capacity crisis 
   142                  continues. In addition, the exclusion of certain 
   143                  countries
   144  
   145  [[Page 9808]]
   146  
   147                  and products from the tariff and efforts by foreign 
   148                  producers to circumvent the tariff have undermined the 
   149                  purpose of Proclamation 9704, which was to adjust the 
   150                  level of imports of aluminum to remove the threatened 
   151                  impairment of the national security. This has again 
   152                  resulted in aluminum smelter capacity utilization rates 
   153                  in the domestic aluminum industry that are well below 
   154                  the target level recommended in the Secretary's January 
   155                  19, 2018, report. This indicates that the initial 
   156                  tariff of 10 percent ad valorem is not high enough to 
   157                  address the threatened impairment to our national 
   158                  security posed by aluminum imports.
   159  
   160                  6. In particular, the Secretary has informed me that 
   161                  global primary aluminum capacity has continued to 
   162                  increase, fueled by expansions in the People's Republic 
   163                  of China (China) and South America, which is seen in 
   164                  rising aluminum imports that continue to weigh on the 
   165                  price domestic aluminum producers may charge. There has 
   166                  also been a significant increase in Chinese investment 
   167                  in Mexico, driven by massive Chinese government 
   168                  subsidies and the continued ability to exploit 
   169                  loopholes in U.S. trade policy.
   170  
   171                  7. Domestic aluminum producers have been forced to idle 
   172                  additional production and shut down facilities. Two 
   173                  primary aluminum smelters within the United States have 
   174                  closed since Proclamation 9704 was promulgated. In 
   175                  addition, U.S. primary aluminum production decreased by 
   176                  30 percent from 2020 to 2024, and U.S. smelter capacity 
   177                  utilization was only 52 percent in 2024. Overcapacity 
   178                  for primary aluminum has harmed downstream aluminum 
   179                  producers, including producers of aluminum extrusions 
   180                  and aluminum sheet. To allow U.S. aluminum producers to 
   181                  restart production and to incentivize new capacity, 
   182                  additional adjustments to section 232 tariffs on 
   183                  aluminum need to be made, including limiting exemptions 
   184                  and increasing the tariff rate.
   185  
   186                  8. The Secretary has informed me that imports of 
   187                  aluminum articles from countries that are excluded from 
   188                  the tariff regime or have alternative arrangements have 
   189                  remained significantly elevated at levels that once 
   190                  again threaten to impair the national security of the 
   191                  United States. The volume of U.S. imports of aluminum 
   192                  articles from Argentina, Australia, Canada, Mexico, EU 
   193                  countries, and the UK in 2024 was approximately 14 
   194                  percent higher than the average volume of such imports 
   195                  in 2015 through 2017. In particular, the volume of U.S. 
   196                  imports of primary aluminum from Canada in 2024 was 
   197                  approximately 18 percent higher than the average volume 
   198                  for 2015 through 2017. Notwithstanding Proclamation 
   199                  10782 of July 10, 2024, which imposed higher tariffs on 
   200                  certain aluminum imports from Mexico, imports of 
   201                  aluminum from Mexico have continued to surge beyond 
   202                  historical volumes. The volume of U.S. imports of 
   203                  aluminum articles from Mexico in 2024 was approximately 
   204                  35 percent higher than the average volume for 2015 
   205                  through 2017. Proclamation 10782 did not resolve the 
   206                  surge of imports of aluminum from Mexico. Mexican 
   207                  producers are using unfair trade to gain market share 
   208                  in the United States and are leveraging their access to 
   209                  unfairly traded global primary aluminum to do so. I 
   210                  understand that Mexican producers are commingling 
   211                  primary aluminum from China and the Russian Federation 
   212                  (Russia) with primary aluminum from other countries to 
   213                  produce downstream aluminum articles. These practices 
   214                  are distortive and provide continued outlets to absorb 
   215                  the massive amount of global excess capacity and must 
   216                  be remedied. The volume of U.S. imports of primary 
   217                  aluminum from Australia has also surged and in 2024 was 
   218                  approximately 103 percent higher than the average 
   219                  volume for 2015 through 2017. Australia has disregarded 
   220                  its verbal commitment to voluntarily restrain its 
   221                  aluminum exports to a reasonable level.
   222  
   223                  9. These volume increases occurred even though demand 
   224                  for aluminum in the United States and Canada (the 
   225                  market measured by industry) has generally remained 
   226                  flat, averaging about 20 percent since 2018.
   227  
   228                  10. These increasing import volumes support the 
   229                  conclusion that aluminum producers in countries subject 
   230                  to the additional ad valorem tariff proclaimed in 
   231                  Proclamation 9704 are engaging in transshipment or 
   232                  further processing
   233  
   234  [[Page 9809]]
   235  
   236                  of upstream aluminum products in countries that have 
   237                  since been exempted from that tariff. Foreign producers 
   238                  have shifted assembly or manufacturing operations to 
   239                  third countries, such as Mexico. For example, Chinese 
   240                  producers are using Mexico's general exclusion from the 
   241                  tariff to funnel Chinese aluminum to the United States 
   242                  through Mexico while avoiding the tariff.
   243  
   244                  11. The Secretary has informed me that producers in 
   245                  countries that remain subject to the ad valorem tariff 
   246                  have continued to evade the tariff by processing 
   247                  covered aluminum articles into additional downstream 
   248                  derivative products that were not included in the 
   249                  additional ad valorem tariffs proclaimed in 
   250                  Proclamation 9704 and Proclamation 9980. Foreign

    34                  By the President of the United States of America

    37  
    38                  1. On January 11, 2018, the Secretary of Commerce 
    39                  (Secretary) transmitted to me a report on the 
    40                  Secretary's investigation into the effect of imports of 
    41                  steel mill articles (steel articles) on the national 
    42                  security of the United States under section 232 of the 
    43                  Trade Expansion Act of 1962, as amended (19 U.S.C. 
    44                  1862) (section 232). The Secretary found and advised me 
    45                  of his opinion that steel articles are being imported 
    46                  into the United States in such quantities and under 
    47                  such circumstances as to threaten to impair the 
    48                  national security of the United States.
    49  
    50                  2. In Proclamation 9705 of March 8, 2018 (Adjusting 
    51                  Imports of Steel Into the United States), and 
    52                  Proclamation 9980 of January 24, 2020 (Adjusting 
    53                  Imports of Derivative Aluminum Articles and Derivative 
    54                  Steel Articles Into the United States), I concurred 
    55                  with the Secretary's findings that steel articles, as 
    56                  defined in clause 1 of Proclamation 9705, and 
    57                  derivative steel articles, as described in clause 3 of 
    58                  Proclamation 9980, are being imported into the United

    60                  as to threaten to impair the national security of the 
    61                  United States, and I decided to adjust the imports of 
    62                  those steel articles and derivative steel articles by 
    63                  imposing a 25 percent ad valorem tariff on such 
    64                  articles imported from most countries. In Proclamation 
    65                  10896 of February 10, 2025 (Adjusting Imports of Steel 
    66                  Into the United States), I decided to adjust the 
    67                  imports of steel articles and derivative steel articles 
    68                  by imposing a 25 percent ad valorem tariff on such 
    69                  articles imported from all countries.
    70  
    71                  3. On January 19, 2018, the Secretary transmitted to me 
    72                  a report on the Secretary's investigation into the 
    73                  effect of imports of aluminum articles on the national 
    74                  security of the United States under section 232. The 
    75                  Secretary found and advised me of his opinion that 
    76                  aluminum articles are being imported into the United 
    77                  States in such quantities and under such circumstances 
    78                  as to threaten to impair the national security of the 
    79                  United States.
    80  
    81                  4. In Proclamation 9704 of March 8, 2018 (Adjusting 
    82                  Imports of Aluminum Into the United States), and 
    83                  Proclamation 9980, I concurred with the Secretary's 
    84                  findings that aluminum articles, as defined in clause 1 
    85                  of Proclamation 9704, and derivative aluminum articles, 
    86                  as described in clause 3 of Proclamation 9980, are 
    87                  being imported into the United States in such 
    88                  quantities and under such circumstances as to threaten 
    89                  to impair the national security of the United States, 
    90                  and decided to adjust the imports of aluminum articles 
    91                  and derivative aluminum articles by imposing a 10 
    92                  percent ad valorem tariff on such articles imported 
    93                  from most countries. In Proclamation 10895 of February 
    94                  10, 2025 (Adjusting Imports of Aluminum Into the United 
    95                  States), I decided to adjust the imports of aluminum 
    96                  articles and derivative aluminum articles by imposing a 
    97                  25 percent ad valorem tariff on such articles imported 
    98                  from all countries.
    99  
   100                  5. In Proclamation 10896 and Proclamation 10895, I 
   101                  instructed the Secretary to continue to monitor imports 
   102                  of steel articles and derivative steel articles, and 
   103                  aluminum articles and derivative aluminum articles, 
   104                  respectively, and
   105  
   106  [[Page 24200]]
   107  
   108                  to review the status of such imports with respect to 
   109                  the national security of the United States. The 
   110                  Secretary has done so and has advised me accordingly.
   111  
   112                  6. After considering current information newly provided 
   113                  by the Secretary, among other things, I have determined 
   114                  that it is necessary to increase the previously 
   115                  described steel and aluminum tariffs to adjust the 
   116                  imports of steel and aluminum articles and their 
   117                  derivative articles so that such imports will not 
   118                  threaten to impair the national security. In my 
   119                  judgment, the increased tariffs will more effectively 
   120                  counter foreign countries that continue to offload low-
   121                  priced, excess steel and aluminum in the United States 
   122                  market and thereby undercut the competitiveness of the 
   123                  United States steel and aluminum industries. Although 
   124                  the previously imposed steel and aluminum tariffs have 
   125                  helped provide critical price support in the United 
   126                  States market, they have not yet enabled these 
   127                  industries to develop and maintain the rates of 
   128                  capacity production utilization that are necessary for 
   129                  the industries' sustained health and for projected 
   130                  national defense needs. I have determined that 
   131                  increasing the previously imposed tariffs will provide 
   132                  greater support to these industries and reduce or 
   133                  eliminate the national security threat posed by imports 
   134                  of steel and aluminum articles and their derivative 
   135                  articles.
   136  
   137                  7. Accordingly, I have determined that it is necessary 
   138                  and appropriate to increase the tariff rate for imports 
   139                  of steel articles and derivative steel articles, and 
   140                  aluminum articles and derivative aluminum articles, 
   141                  from 25 percent ad valorem to 50 percent ad valorem 
   142                  effective as of 12:01 a.m. eastern daylight time on

   144                  necessary and appropriate to modify the way in which

   156                  and to accordingly provide different treatment, as 
   157                  described below, for imports of steel and aluminum 
   158                  articles, and their derivatives, from the United 
   159                  Kingdom.
   160

   162                  imports of an article and its derivatives that are 
   163                  being imported into the United States in such 
   164                  quantities or under such circumstances as to threaten 
   165                  to impair the national security.
   166  
   167                  9. Section 604 of the Trade Act of 1974, as amended (19

   187                  9704, as amended; Proclamation 9705, as amended;

tools.name: fr_search

query.description: Full-text search terms; "" for none. Supports quoted phrases, e.g. "\"extension of stay\" F-1".
query.title: Query

doc_type.description: Document types: RULE, PRORULE (proposed rule), NOTICE, PRESDOCU (presidential document). null for all.
doc_type.title: Doc Type

agency.description: Agency slugs, e.g. homeland-security-department, u-s-citizenship-and-immigration-services, u-s-immigration-and-customs-enforcement, state-department, labor-department, executive-office-of-the-president.
agency.title: Agency

pres_type.description: Presidential document subtypes (use with doc_type PRESDOCU).
pres_type.title: Pres Type

cfr.description: CFR title:part affected, e.g. 8:214. The part must be numeric; lettered parts are not supported by this filter.
cfr.title: Cfr

tools.description: Search U.S. Federal Register documents (rules, proposed rules, notices, presidential documents) by keywords and filters. Prints document numbers, titles, types, dates, citations, dockets, RINs and abstracts.

tools.name: fr_doc
tools.description: Metadata for one Federal Register document: title, type, action, citation, page range, publication/signing/effective dates, comment deadline, docket, RIN, CFR parts affected, corrections, abstract.

tools.name: fr_toc
tools.description: Outline of a document's full text: headings with line numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_grep

pattern.description: Python regular expression, searched over the whole text (a match may span lines). ^ and $ match at line boundaries; . does not match a newline.
pattern.title: Pattern

context.description: Lines of context around each match (default 2, at most 10).
context.title: Context

tools.description: Regex search inside one document's full text. Shows the lines of each match with line numbers, context lines and the FR page of each match. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_text
tools.description: Read a document's full text by line range, with line numbers. [[Page N]] markers give FR page numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

answer.description: Direct answer to each lettered part, in order, labelled (a), (b), ...
answer.title: Answer

basis.description: Provisions and documents relied on, with citations.
basis.title: Basis

uncertainty.description: What the documents leave open, or "None".
uncertainty.title: Uncertainty

**Analyzing enforcement failures**

I see there's a contradiction in the USTR's overall summary. It states that all investigated economies failed to impose and enforce a forced labor import prohibition. But in earlier findings, it mentioned that six economies had imposed something, yet they weren't enforcing it effectively. This inconsistency raises questions for me about how these assessments are being made and what the implications are for addressing forced labor issues globally.

**Planning document structure**

I need to reference a "dairy scope" that's missing and estimate the time budget at 60k, but it looks like I might output around 15k tokens, which should be fine. I need to comply with a structured format in JSON, ensuring no extra wrappers and using escaped strings. I could synthesize this concisely. My plan includes a table where each row has formulas and zeros, along with an explanatory legend encoded by date. Each line will also list relevant codes with calculations repeated as needed.**Structuring the table**

I'm planning to show the 232s with formulas and a legend, using "$100,000 × 0%" to represent zeros across the entire table, along with positive calculations when common. Each instruction will require one line per duty layer for every duty amount. I’ll use a 14-row table, merging rows with the same cases for ease. This will feature columns for six taxes, and I’ll add compact codes and reasons grouped by timelines throughout. Each row will detail amounts, ensuring clarity on exemptions and changes.**Clarifying amounts**

I need to round amounts that I mention, especially regarding historical context. I must note that any action related to 232 before March 12 isn't valid, with 25k as the expected default. Q11.answer:
The following are text-based discrepancies or tensions, distinguished from ordinary prospective amendments:

1. Proposal's location of exemptions. The June notice says the proposed exemptions 'in Annex A' include all articles and parts currently subject to section 232 tariffs, and also describes informational materials and donations among proposed exemptions. But Annex A's readable introductory note says those categories are excluded 'in addition to the products listed in this Annex.' Both passages describe the proposal, not a later policy change (FR Doc. 2026-11296, 91 FR 34274, 34276).

2. Dairy scope reference. The dairy exclusion's operative clause (3) refers to a September 8 proclamation modifying the scope of the dairy duties. The published September 8 scope proclamations are for alcoholic beverages and motor vehicles, not dairy; no dairy scope proclamation was found through today (FR Doc. 2026-18836, 91 FR 58320; FR Docs. 2026-18838 and 2026-18839, 91 FR 58331, 58339).

3. Description of the 60 economies. The July action notice says all investigated economies 'have failed to impose a forced labor import prohibition and to effectively enforce such a prohibition,' and parenthetically says all failed 'both factors.' Its preceding list says six failed to effectively enforce; the June proposal expressly identifies those six as economies that impose a prohibition (FR Doc. 2026-15181, 91 FR 47318; FR Doc. 2026-11296, 91 FR 34274). Read literally as failure of each individual factor, the July sentence conflicts; read as failure to satisfy the combined two-factor test, it can be reconciled.

4. Printed start date after suspension. Original operative clauses and recitals print August 19, while the later suspension's operative clause sets August 22 and amends the Annex II chapeaux, not those printed clauses. Later proclamations also recount the original August 19 date before describing the suspension and August 22 start. This is a textual tension resolved by the later operative amendment and supersession, not evidence that both dates governed entries (FR Docs. 2026-14991, 91 FR 46640–41; 2026-17294, 91 FR 54790–91; 2026-18835, 91 FR 58311).

Q11.uncertainty: The third item admits a reconciliatory reading. The fourth is an expressly resolved amendment rather than an unexplained change. Image-only product-list comparisons cannot be independently assessed.

Q12.answer:
(a) Aloe, Tasmanian pepper, coconut and centella extracts: Cambodia $60,000 × 0% = $0; Malaysia $60,000 × 10% = $6,000.

(b) Boswellia: Malaysia $100,000 × 0% = $0; Taiwan $100,000 × 0% = $0; Bangladesh $100,000 × 10% = $10,000; Argentina $100,000 × 10% = $10,000.

(c) Argan oil: Taiwan $100,000 × 0% = $0; Japan $100,000 × (12.5% − 4%) = $8,500; Indonesia $100,000 × 10% = $10,000.

(d) Sesame seeds for sowing: Japan, Mexico and Thailand each owe $50,000 × 0% = $0 under the product-specific general exemption.

(e) Psyllium seed husks: Cambodia $40,000 × 0% = $0; Thailand $40,000 × 12.5% = $5,000; El Salvador $40,000 × 10% = $4,000; Italy $40,000 × (10% − 2%) = $3,200.
Q12.uncertainty: The negative conclusions use the scenario's assumption that the articles are not on any image-only list. The specific exemptions depend on both description and country.

Q13.answer:
(a) Non-U.S. content: $200,000 − $60,000 = $140,000. Section 232: $140,000 × 25% = $35,000; the full-value floor is $200,000 × 15% = $30,000. Duty: $35,000.

(b) $200,000 non-U.S. content × 25% = $50,000; above the $30,000 floor. Duty: $50,000.

(c) No USMCA qualification: $200,000 × 25% = $50,000.

(d) Japan: $200,000 × (15% − 2.5% column-1 rate) = $25,000 section 232.

(e) October 20: U.S. content is $20,000 in U.S.-produced parts plus $30,000 in qualifying U.S.-smelted and cast aluminum, without double counting. Non-U.S. content is $200,000 − $50,000 = $150,000. $150,000 × 25% = $37,500, above the $30,000 floor. Duty: $37,500.

(f) October 6, before the Commerce guidance's effective date: using the proclamation's parts-produced-in-the-United-States definition, ($200,000 − $20,000) × 25% = $45,000; above the $30,000 floor.

(g) ($200,000 − $140,000) × 25% = $15,000, but the floor is $200,000 × 15% = $30,000. Duty: $30,000.

(h) The clause (2) treatment lasts through 11:59 p.m. Eastern standard time December 31, 2027. From 12:01 a.m. January 1, 2028, clause (3) directs the rates in Proclamation 11021, clause (3); on the stated facts the general 25% rate would be $200,000 × 25% = $50,000, subject to any later change.
Q13.basis: FR Doc. 2026-11314, clauses (2)(a)–(d), (3)–(4), 91 FR 34087–88; FR Doc. 2026-20938, DATES and guidance paragraphs 1–2, 91 FR 65162; FR Doc. 2026-06960, clause (3), 91 FR 18204.
Q13.uncertainty: The October 14 guidance is expressly prospective; it does not say whether the same valuation of U.S. metal was permissible before that date. The October 6 calculation follows the narrower express wording of the proclamation. Annex IV details are image-only.

Q14.answer:
1. Incorrect. The memorandum's recital reports USTR's prediction of feasibility by September 1, but section 2 directs establishment as soon as USTR determines it feasible; it sets no September 1 deadline.

2. Partly correct. 'Over 450' is true but understates the reported over 1,600 written comments; 'nearly 60 witnesses' is wrong—the notice reports over 100.

3. Incorrect. Six economies adopted bans and Jordan undertook an ART commitment. Cambodia and Guatemala were already proposed at 10%; the other five of the seven moved from proposed 12.5% to 10%.

4. Incorrect. Commenters raised objections; USTR expressly decided not to remove the products, including beef and avocados, from the proposed exemptions. The notice links the forced-labor allegation to beef; its avocado discussion concerns pressure from imports.

5. Incorrect. Japan and South Korea have net-of-MFN treatment but no separate negotiated product part in the notice's Annex II table of contents. The EU, Switzerland and Taiwan do have economy-specific parts.

6. Partly correct. USTR says it added 471 products in each investigation, but describes certain sugar and sugar-containing products, including certain in-quota imports, not all sugar products.

7. Incorrect. USTR refers to 'maximum tariffs of 12.5 percent' in discussing this action. It does not cap all duties in total: the note generally adds section 301 to MFN and other applicable duties; MFN itself can exceed a netting cap.

8. Correct with its qualification: the notice requires privileged foreign status for goods subject to the action, except goods eligible for domestic status.

9. Correct as the stated severability rule: the applicable tariff applies to imports covered by an invalidated exemption; other exemptions remain operative. Another independently applicable exemption would still need consideration.

10. Partly correct as a description of USTR's statement, but not independently verifiable from the readable product tables. USTR says it retained all products proposed in Annex A except non-pharmaceutical applications of certain chemicals. The proposal separately described additional categorical exclusions, including section 232 goods, and the adopted readable note is narrower for section 232.
Q14.uncertainty: Statement 10 cannot be audited product-by-product because the proposal and adopted classification tables are images. The separate categorical section 232 exclusion should not be conflated with the image list itself.

Q15.answer:
All calculations below are additional to MFN. Each rate is applied to the stated $100,000; thus 25% = $25,000 and 50% = $50,000. Case N does not qualify for USMCA; Case U qualifies and claims it. The table gives the best reading of duties legally owed today, not historical deposits.

| Entry date | Section 232: N / U | Section 338: N / U | Total: N / U |
|---|---|---|---|
| Feb. 10, 2025 | 0% = $0 / $0 | Not yet imposed | $0 / $0 |
| Mar. 6, 2025 | 0% = $0 / $0 | Not yet imposed | $0 / $0 |
| Mar. 10, 2025 | 0% = $0 / $0 | Not yet imposed | $0 / $0 |
| Mar. 14, 2025 | 25% = $25,000* / $25,000 | Not yet imposed | $25,000* / $25,000 |
| Jun. 3, 2025 | 25% = $25,000* / $25,000 | Not yet imposed | $25,000* / $25,000 |
| Jun. 10, 2025 | 50% = $50,000 / $50,000 | Not yet imposed | $50,000 / $50,000 |
| Aug. 5, 2025 | 50% = $50,000 / $50,000 | Not yet imposed | $50,000 / $50,000 |
| Mar. 2, 2026 | 50% = $50,000 / $50,000 | Not yet imposed | $50,000 / $50,000 |
| Jun. 10, 2026 | 50% = $50,000 / $50,000 | Not yet imposed | $50,000 / $50,000 |
| Jul. 27, 2026 | 50% = $50,000 / $50,000 | Not yet effective | $50,000 / $50,000 |
| Aug. 25, 2026 | 50% = $50,000 / $50,000 | 0% = $0 / $0 | $50,000 / $50,000 |
| Sept. 14, 2026 | 50% = $50,000 / $50,000 | 0% = $0 / $0 | $50,000 / $50,000 |
| Sept. 16, 2026 | 50% = $50,000 / $50,000 | 50% = $50,000 / $50,000 | $100,000 / $100,000 |
| Nov. 10, 2026 | 50% = $50,000 / $50,000 | 50% = $50,000 / $50,000 | $100,000 / $100,000 |

Other layers for each relevant period, in both cases:
- Northern-border IEEPA: $100,000 × 0% = $0 on February 10 because it was paused; $0 on the 2025 dates as legally owed today because CBP reports the Supreme Court held IEEPA tariffs unlawful; $0 on every 2026 date after the ruling and termination. Historically, the order had prescribed 25% from March 4, with the USMCA free-entry exception from March 7, and 35% for covered non-USMCA goods from August 1.
- Reciprocal IEEPA: $100,000 × 0% = $0 on all listed dates. Before April 2025 it did not exist; later it was unlawful as reported by CBP, and the order also addressed Canadian goods and section 232 articles separately.
- Section 122 surcharge: $100,000 × 0% = $0 before February 24, 2026 and after its July 24 endpoint. On March 2 and June 10, 2026, $100,000 × 0% = $0 because section 232 applies to the full value; Case U also meets the stated USMCA free-entry exception.
- Forced-labor section 301: $100,000 × 0% = $0 before July 24, 2026. On July 27 and each later date, $100,000 × 0% = $0 because the article is entered under the specified aluminum section 232 heading in note 52(f)(1); Case U also has the USMCA free-entry exception.
- Section 338: not yet effective before August 22, 2026; on August 25 and September 14 the original section 232 exclusion applies. From September 15, the motor-vehicles scope proclamation expressly makes section 338 additive to section 232.

*For Case N on March 14 and June 3, the $25,000 figure treats the now-unlawful IEEPA tariff as unable to trigger the old non-stacking rule. A materially different reading treats the historical entry as having been 'subject to' that tariff when entered, preserving the then-applicable section 232 waiver: that would yield $100,000 × 0% = $0 section 232 and a $0 additional-duty total for those two N entries. The Federal Register materials found do not resolve that retroactive interaction.
Q15.uncertainty: The FR reports the Supreme Court ruling and describes refund orders for unliquidated and nonfinal entries, but does not resolve whether an unlawful historical IEEPA assessment still triggers the retroactive non-stacking waiver for Case N on March 14 and June 3. Final liquidation and refund eligibility are also not supplied. The cited CBP notice says remaining section 232 duties are retained and collected, but does not specifically decide this interaction. The June 2026 Annex I-C preferential-content rule does not apply to these extrusions under the stated list assumptions.

Q1.answer:
All times below are Eastern. The three original proclamations were signed July 20 and published July 23, 2026. Their printed start was August 19; Proclamation 11056 changed the operative start to August 22.

| Proclamation | FR document; first page | Signed; published | Action and operative event |
|---|---|---|---|
| 11046 | 2026-14991; 91 FR 46639 | Jul. 20; Jul. 23 | 50% on listed Canadian alcoholic products; consumption entry or warehouse withdrawal from 12:01 a.m. Aug. 19 as printed, changed to Aug. 22. |
| 11047 | 2026-14992; 91 FR 46653 | Jul. 20; Jul. 23 | Same duty and entry-based dates for listed dairy products. |
| 11048 | 2026-14997; 91 FR 46663 | Jul. 20; Jul. 23 | Same duty and entry-based dates for listed motor-vehicles-action products. |
| 11056 | 2026-17294; 91 FR 54789 | Aug. 18; Aug. 24 | Changes the three duty effective dates to 12:01 a.m. Aug. 22, measured against consumption entry or withdrawal. |
| 11061 | 2026-18835; 91 FR 58311 | Sept. 8; Sept. 14 | Excludes listed alcoholic beverages imported from 12:01 a.m. Sept. 29; the event is importation, not consumption entry. |
| 11062 | 2026-18836; 91 FR 58319 | Sept. 8; Sept. 14 | Corresponding dairy-product exclusion, measured by importation from 12:01 a.m. Sept. 29. |
| 11063 | 2026-18837; 91 FR 58325 | Sept. 8; Sept. 14 | Corresponding motor-vehicles-action exclusion, measured by importation from 12:01 a.m. Sept. 29. |
| 11064 | 2026-18838; 91 FR 58331 | Sept. 8; Sept. 14 | Adds Part A and removes Part B alcoholic products from the duty; makes the modified duty additive to section 232. Applies to entries or withdrawals from 12:01 a.m. Sept. 15. |
| 11065 | 2026-18839; 91 FR 58339 | Sept. 8; Sept. 14 | Adds Part A and removes Part B motor-vehicles-action products; makes the modified duty additive to section 232. Same entry-based Sept. 15 time. |
| 11076 | 2026-22292; 91 FR 68861 | Oct. 23; Oct. 30 | Removes Part A and adds Part B motor-vehicles-action products; applies to entries or withdrawals from 12:01 a.m. Oct. 30. |

Product scope: alcoholic beverages were first listed by 11046, changed by 11064, and partially excluded from importation by 11061. Dairy was first listed by 11047 and partially excluded by 11062. Motor-vehicles-action products were first listed by 11048, changed by 11065 and 11076, and partially excluded by 11063. The suspension changed timing, not product lists.
Q1.uncertainty: Proclamation 11062, clause (3), refers to a September 8 dairy scope proclamation. No such proclamation was found in the Federal Register series through November 14. Its reference does not establish an independently verifiable change to the dairy list. Annex product tables are images.

Q2.answer:
(a) Entry 1: $40,000 × 0% = $0. Entry 2: $40,000 × 0% = $0. Entry 3: $40,000 × 50% = $20,000. The change occurs at 12:01 a.m. August 22, not at the close of that day.

(b) Proclamation 11056, clause (1), expressly sets August 22 and substitutes that date in the chapeau of Annex II of each original proclamation. It does not literally amend the August 19 text in clauses (1) and (3) or the recital of Proclamation 11046. Its later operative date and clause (5)'s supersession of inconsistent prior provisions resolve the difference.

(c) The deposited $20,000 is not the duty due under the changed effective date. To the extent implementation requires a refund, Proclamation 11056, clause (4), calls for processing under applicable law and CBP's standard procedures; it does not specify a deadline or an automatic payment.

(d) No further presidential action was needed: the suspension expired by its own terms. Later recitals say Canada reneged and ceased negotiating in good faith on August 21, and the suspension lapsed and duties became effective at 12:01 a.m. August 22.

(e) The original finding was signed July 20. July 20 + 30 days = August 19. The proclamation describes section 338 as forbidding the additional duties from taking effect earlier than 30 days after the finding proclamation.
Q2.basis: FR Doc. 2026-14991, recital 10 and clauses (1), (3), 91 FR 46640–42; FR Doc. 2026-17294, recitals 4–5 and clauses (1), (4)–(5), 91 FR 54790–91; FR Doc. 2026-18835, recitals 2–4, 91 FR 58311.
Q2.uncertainty: The proclamation states the refund rule but does not determine the entry's liquidation status or a particular procedural route.

Q3.answer:
(a) A: importation and entry are permitted; $30,000 × 50% = $15,000. B: the September 27 importation precedes the ban; the October 5 warehouse withdrawal remains subject to $30,000 × 50% = $15,000. C: importation at 11:30 p.m. September 28 precedes the ban; the later entry remains subject to $30,000 × 50% = $15,000. D: importation at 12:30 a.m. September 29 is excluded; no lawful consumption-entry duty total is calculated.

(b) E was imported before the ban. The most defensible reading is that it is not barred merely because consumption entry from the zone occurs October 6, and remains subject to $30,000 × 50% = $15,000. When admitted on September 25, a duty-subject article had to be admitted in privileged foreign status unless eligible for domestic status.

(c) If the ban is invalidated as applied to the beer, Proclamation 11061, clause (9)(b), makes the 50% duty apply to the import to which the invalidated ban applied: $30,000 × 50% = $15,000 on the stated value.

(d) No. Apart from switching its Annex products from duty to exclusion, the exclusion proclamation leaves the other duty-covered products as established by the alcoholic-beverages scope proclamation.
Q3.uncertainty: The exclusion's grandfathering clause expressly mentions unentered and warehouse goods, not foreign-trade-zone withdrawals. The scenario defines importation as physical arrival, supporting the stated reading for E, but the text does not separately resolve every zone-status consequence.

Q4.answer:
(a) September 10, for each X, Y and Z: section 232 is $100,000 × 25% = $25,000; section 338 is $100,000 × 0% = $0. Each original proclamation excludes articles subject to section 232 duties.

(b) October 1:
- X: section 232 $100,000 × 25% = $25,000; section 338 $100,000 × 50% = $50,000.
- Y: section 232 $100,000 × 25% = $25,000; section 338 $100,000 × 0% = $0.
- Z: section 232 $100,000 × 25% = $25,000; section 338 $100,000 × 50% = $50,000.

(c) The original clause (2) says the section 338 duties 'shall not apply to articles subject to duties pursuant to section 232.' The later alcoholic and motor-vehicles scope proclamations say the duties, 'as modified in this proclamation, shall apply in addition to duties imposed pursuant to section 232.' They take effect September 15. No corresponding dairy modification was found.
Q4.uncertainty: The dairy exclusion proclamation refers to a dairy scope proclamation that was not found. The answer uses the operative documents actually published through today.

Q5.answer:
(a) 'Yes' means the 50% duty applies to the entry. Columns are Sept. 14 3 p.m.; Sept. 15 12:01 a.m.; Oct. 29 4 p.m.; Oct. 30 12:01 a.m.; Nov. 3.

| Product | Five answers, in order | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| P | No; yes; yes; yes; yes | September Part A adds it. |
| Q | Yes; no; no; no; no | September Part B removes it. |
| R | Yes; yes; yes; no; no | October Part A removes it. |
| S | No; no; no; yes; yes | October Part B adds it. |

(b) Proclamation 11076 was signed October 23, filed October 29 at 11:15 a.m., and published October 30, 2026. It applies from 12:01 a.m. October 30 to consumption entries and warehouse withdrawals. The September and October scope changes are prospective by those terms; neither provides a refund for earlier entries.

(c) P and S each became dutiable seven calendar days after the relevant scope proclamation was signed. Each scope proclamation repeats the 30-day description of section 338 but does not explain its application to newly added products. The original motor-vehicles finding was signed July 20—57 days before September 15 and 102 days before October 30.
Q5.basis: FR Doc. 2026-14997, clause (1), 91 FR 46665, as delayed by 2026-17294, clause (1), 91 FR 54790; FR Doc. 2026-18839, recital 8 and clauses (1)–(2), 91 FR 58340; FR Doc. 2026-22292, recital 9 and clauses (1)–(2), 91 FR 68862, and filing line at 91 FR 68871.
Q5.uncertainty: The proclamations do not expressly explain whether the original July finding satisfies the waiting period for products added later. The table applies the operative effective dates without resolving that legal question.

Q6.answer:
(a) MFN is $100,000 × 4% = $4,000 in each case. Section 301 and the requested MFN-plus-section-301 total are:

| Product of | Section 301 calculation | Total |
|---|---:|---:|

| Norway | $100,000 × 12.5% = $12,500 | $16,500 |
| United Kingdom | $100,000 × 10% = $10,000 | $14,000 |
| Germany | $100,000 × 6% = $6,000 | $10,000 |
| Taiwan | $100,000 × 6% = $6,000 | $10,000 |
| Türkiye | $100,000 × 12.5% = $12,500 | $16,500 |
| Japan | $100,000 × 8.5% = $8,500 | $12,500 |

| Hong Kong | $100,000 × 12.5% = $12,500 | $16,500 |

(b) Section 301 only: Germany, $100,000 × 0% = $0; Japan, $100,000 × (12.5% − 12%) = $500; Taiwan, $100,000 × 0% = $0; South Korea, $100,000 × (12.5% − 10%) = $2,500; duty-free Switzerland, $100,000 × 12.5% = $12,500.

(c) The June proposal was a flat additional 10% for the EU and Taiwan; the adopted treatment nets MFN against 10%. It proposed a flat additional 12.5% for Japan and Switzerland; the adopted treatment nets MFN against 12.5%. The stated reason for netting was consistency with agreements or similar arrangements and encouragement of forced-labor commitments or prohibitions. Q6.basis: FR Doc. 2026-11296, section IV, 91 FR 34274; FR Doc. 2026-15274, economy list, 91 FR 47717–18, and section 1(a), 91 FR 47720; FR Doc. 2026-15181, sections I and II.A, 91 FR 47318–21.
Q6.uncertainty: The answers assume no applicable image-list exemption, as specified. The netting cap concerns MFN plus this section 301 duty, not every possible duty.

Q7.answer:
(a) France: MFN is 2,000 kg × $0.03 = $60; $60 ÷ $12,000 = 0.5%. Section 301 is $12,000 × (10% − 0.5%) = $1,140.

(b) MFN is $20,000 × 4% = $800, plus 4,000 kg × $0.25 = $1,000, or $1,800 ÷ $20,000 = 9%. Italy: $20,000 × (10% − 9%) = $200. Japan: $20,000 × (12.5% − 9%) = $700. Brazil: $20,000 × 12.5% = $2,500.

(c) The MFN equivalent is $2,200 ÷ $20,000 = 11%. Taiwan: $20,000 × 0% = $0, because 11% exceeds its 10% cap. Switzerland: $20,000 × (12.5% − 11%) = $300.

(d) The conversion rule is in new chapter 99 U.S. note 52(k), in Annex I of the action notice. The zero result at or above the applicable cap is stated expressly in section 1(a)(ii) of the presidential memorandum and in the notice's economy determinations.
Q7.basis: FR Doc. 2026-15181, Annex I, note 52(k), 91 FR 47394, and sections II.A–B, 91 FR 47320–28; FR Doc. 2026-15274, section 1(a)(ii), 91 FR 47720.

Q8.answer:
(a) Section 301, in order:
1. $80,000 × 12.5% = $10,000: entry is not before July 28.
2. $80,000 × 0% = $0: qualifying vessel transit and entry before July 28.
3. $80,000 × 12.5% = $10,000: the exception ended at 12:01 a.m. July 28.
4. $80,000 × 12.5% = $10,000: loading was after the July 24 cutoff.
5. $80,000 × 0% = $0: entry preceded the effective time.
6. $80,000 × 12.5% = $10,000: withdrawal occurred after the start, with no qualifying transit shown.
7. $80,000 × 12.5% = $10,000: aircraft loading does not meet the DATES line's vessel requirement.

(b) The transit exception is in the DATES line of FR Doc. 2026-15181, 91 FR 47318. It requires both vessel loading and final-mode transit before 12:01 a.m. July 24, and entry or warehouse withdrawal before 12:01 a.m. July 28.

(c) The memorandum was signed July 23. The notice makes duties applicable from 12:01 a.m. Eastern July 24, subject to the transit exception; the action notice was published July 28.

(d) July 30: $80,000 × 12.5% = $10,000. August 3: $80,000 × 0% = $0. The specific exemption for patented pharmaceutical articles under headings 9903.04.60–9903.04.66 begins July 31.
Q8.basis: FR Doc. 2026-15181, DATES and Dominican Republic determination, 91 FR 47318, 47323; Annex I, Part B, adding note 52(f)(8), 91 FR 47394; FR Doc. 2026-15274, 91 FR 47717.
Q8.uncertainty: The July 30 calculation assumes no other exemption, including an image-list exemption, as specified in the scenario.

Q9.answer:
(a) Thailand: ($100,000 − $35,000) × 12.5% = $8,125.

(b) Israel: $6,000 repair value × 12.5% = $750; the returned machine's full $150,000 is not the section 301 base.

(c) Mexico: (i) USMCA free entry, $50,000 × 0% = $0; (ii) no USMCA claim, $50,000 × 10% = $5,000.

(d) Japanese passenger car under 9903.94.01: $40,000 × 0% = $0.

(e) Brazil: $100,000 × 12.5% = $12,500, assuming no other applicable exemption. A section 232 duty under an unmentioned heading is not by itself the categorical exemption described in the adopted note.

(f) The June proposal described an exclusion for all articles and parts subject to section 232 tariffs and for informational materials and donations. The adopted note instead specifies particular section 232 categories and headings, and expressly excludes accompanied personal baggage; it does not provide a readable blanket exclusion for all section 232 goods, informational materials, or donations. Individual goods may nevertheless fall within another applicable exemption.
Q9.basis: FR Doc. 2026-11296, section IV and Annex A explanatory note, 91 FR 34274, 34276; FR Doc. 2026-15181, Annex I, notes 52(a), (f)(2), and (h), 91 FR 47352, 47362–63; country determinations at 91 FR 47323–25.
Q9.uncertainty: The image tables cannot be checked for a particular informational item or donation. The answer does not infer that all such goods are necessarily dutiable.

Q10.answer:
Scenario 1, Canadian extrusions:

(a) September 10: MFN $200,000 × 3% = $6,000; section 232 $200,000 × 50% = $100,000; section 338 $200,000 × 0% = $0 because the original motor-vehicles duty excludes section 232 articles; section 301 $200,000 × 0% = $0 under note 52(f)(1). Total: $106,000.

(b) September 16: MFN $200,000 × 3% = $6,000; section 232 $200,000 × 50% = $100,000; section 338 $200,000 × 50% = $100,000 after the stacking change; section 301 $200,000 × 0% = $0. Total: $206,000.

Scenario 2, Canadian whisky:

(c) September 1, USMCA free entry: section 338 $60,000 × 50% = $30,000; section 301 $60,000 × 0% = $0. Total: $30,000.

(d) September 1, no USMCA claim: section 338 $60,000 × 50% = $30,000; section 301 $60,000 × 10% = $6,000. Total: $36,000.

(e) Arrival October 2 is after the September 29 import exclusion. The shipment is barred; there is no lawful entry-duty total to calculate.

(f) Neither the Canada northern-border IEEPA duty nor the temporary section 122 surcharge is in force on September entries. Executive Order 14389 ended the IEEPA tariff actions in February 2026; CBP subsequently reported that the Supreme Court had held IEEPA tariffs unlawful. The 10% surcharge ran from February 24 through the July 24, 2026 endpoint stated in Proclamation 11012; no extension was found.
Q10.uncertainty: The surcharge proclamation states its endpoint as 'through 12:01 a.m.' July 24. That boundary does not affect September. The IEEPA refund consequences of particular historical entries depend on entry status.

Q11.answer:
The following are text-based discrepancies or tensions, distinguished from ordinary prospective amendments:

1. Proposal's location of exemptions. The June notice says the proposed exemptions 'in Annex A' include all articles and parts currently subject to section 232 tariffs, and also describes informational materials and donations among proposed exemptions. But Annex A's readable introductory note says those categories are excluded 'in addition to the products listed in this Annex.' Both passages describe the proposal, not a later policy change (FR Doc. 2026-11296, 91 FR 34274, 34276).

2. Dairy scope reference. The dairy exclusion's operative clause (3) refers to a September 8 proclamation modifying the scope of the dairy duties. The published September 8 scope proclamations are for alcoholic beverages and motor vehicles, not dairy; no dairy scope proclamation was found through today (FR Doc. 2026-18836, 91 FR 58320; FR Docs. 2026-18838 and 2026-18839, 91 FR 58331, 58339).

3. Description of the 60 economies. The July action notice says all investigated economies 'have failed to impose a forced labor import prohibition and to effectively enforce such a prohibition,' and parenthetically says all failed 'both factors.' Its preceding list says six failed to effectively enforce; the June proposal expressly identifies those six as economies that impose a prohibition (FR Doc. 2026-15181, 91 FR 47318; FR Doc. 2026-11296, 91 FR 34274). Read literally as failure of each individual factor, the July sentence conflicts; read as failure to satisfy the combined two-factor test, it can be reconciled.

4. Printed start date after suspension. Original operative clauses and recitals print August 19, while the later suspension's operative clause sets August 22 and amends the Annex II chapeaux, not those printed clauses. Later proclamations also recount the original August 19 date before describing the suspension and August 22 start. This is a textual tension resolved by the later operative amendment and supersession, not evidence that both dates governed entries (FR Docs. 2026-14991, 91 FR 46640–41; 2026-17294, 91 FR 54790–91; 2026-18835, 91 FR 58311).
Q11.basis: The cited passages include proposal explanations and an Annex note, an operative cross-reference, USTR's investigation summary, and presidential operative clauses and recitals. They do not rely on unreadable image tables.
Q11.uncertainty: The third item admits a reconciliatory reading. The fourth is an expressly resolved amendment rather than an unexplained change. Image-only product-list comparisons cannot be independently assessed.

Q13.answer:
(a) Non-U.S. content: $200,000 − $60,000 = $140,000. Section 232: $140,000 × 25% = $35,000; the full-value floor is $200,000 × 15% = $30,000. Duty: $35,000.

(b) $200,000 non-U.S. content × 25% = $50,000; above the $30,000 floor. Duty: $50,000.

(c) No USMCA qualification: $200,000 × 25% = $50,000.

(d) Japan: $200,000 × (15% − 2.5% column-1 rate) = $25,000 section 232.

(e) October 20: U.S. content is $20,000 in U.S.-produced parts plus $30,000 in qualifying U.S.-smelted and cast aluminum, without double counting. Non-U.S. content is $200,000 − $50,000 = $150,000. $150,000 × 25% = $37,500, above the $30,000 floor. Duty: $37,500.

(f) October 6, before the Commerce guidance's effective date: using the proclamation's parts-produced-in-the-United-States definition, ($200,000 − $20,000) × 25% = $45,000; above the $30,000 floor.

(g) ($200,000 − $140,000) × 25% = $15,000, but the floor is $200,000 × 15% = $30,000. Duty: $30,000.

(h) The clause (2) treatment lasts through 11:59 p.m. Eastern standard time December 31, 2027. From 12:01 a.m. January 1, 2028, clause (3) directs the rates in Proclamation 11021, clause (3); on the stated facts the general 25% rate would be $200,000 × 25% = $50,000, subject to any later change.
Q13.basis: FR Doc. 2026-11314, clauses (2)(a)–(d), (3)–(4), 91 FR 34087–88; FR Doc. 2026-20938, DATES and guidance paragraphs 1–2, 91 FR 65162; FR Doc. 2026-06960, clause (3), 91 FR 18204.
Q13.uncertainty: The October 14 guidance is expressly prospective; it does not say whether the same valuation of U.S. metal was permissible before that date. The October 6 calculation follows the narrower express wording of the proclamation. Annex IV details are image-only.

Q14.answer:
1. Incorrect. The memorandum's recital reports USTR's prediction of feasibility by September 1, but section 2 directs establishment as soon as USTR determines it feasible; it sets no September 1 deadline.

2. Partly correct. 'Over 450' is true but understates the reported over 1,600 written comments; 'nearly 60 witnesses' is wrong—the notice reports over 100.

3. Incorrect. Six economies adopted bans and Jordan undertook an ART commitment. Cambodia and Guatemala were already proposed at 10%; the other five of the seven moved from proposed 12.5% to 10%.

4. Incorrect. Commenters raised objections; USTR expressly decided not to remove the products, including beef and avocados, from the proposed exemptions. The notice links the forced-labor allegation to beef; its avocado discussion concerns pressure from imports.

5. Incorrect. Japan and South Korea have net-of-MFN treatment but no separate negotiated product part in the notice's Annex II table of contents. The EU, Switzerland and Taiwan do have economy-specific parts.

6. Partly correct. USTR says it added 471 products in each investigation, but describes certain sugar and sugar-containing products, including certain in-quota imports, not all sugar products.

7. Incorrect. USTR refers to 'maximum tariffs of 12.5 percent' in discussing this action. It does not cap all duties in total: the note generally adds section 301 to MFN and other applicable duties; MFN itself can exceed a netting cap.

8. Correct with its qualification: the notice requires privileged foreign status for goods subject to the action, except goods eligible for domestic status.

9. Correct as the stated severability rule: the applicable tariff applies to imports covered by an invalidated exemption; other exemptions remain operative. Another independently applicable exemption would still need consideration.

10. Partly correct as a description of USTR's statement, but not independently verifiable from the readable product tables. USTR says it retained all products proposed in Annex A except non-pharmaceutical applications of certain chemicals. The proposal separately described additional categorical exclusions, including section 232 goods, and the adopted readable note is narrower for section 232.
Q14.uncertainty: Statement 10 cannot be audited product-by-product because the proposal and adopted classification tables are images. The separate categorical section 232 exclusion should not be conflated with the image list itself.

Other layers for each relevant period, in both cases:
- Northern-border IEEPA: $100,000 × 0% = $0 on February 10 because it was paused; $0 on the 2025 dates as legally owed today because CBP reports the Supreme Court held IEEPA tariffs unlawful; $0 on every 2026 date after the ruling and termination. Historically, the order had prescribed 25% from March 4, with the USMCA free-entry exception from March 7, and 35% for covered non-USMCA goods from August 1.
- Reciprocal IEEPA: $100,000 × 0% = $0 on all listed dates. Before April 2025 it did not exist; later it was unlawful as reported by CBP, and the order also addressed Canadian goods and section 232 articles separately.
- Section 122 surcharge: $100,000 × 0% = $0 before February 24, 2026 and after its July 24 endpoint. On March 2 and June 10, 2026, $100,000 × 0% = $0 because section 232 applies to the full value; Case U also meets the stated USMCA free-entry exception.
- Forced-labor section 301: $100,000 × 0% = $0 before July 24, 2026. On July 27 and each later date, $100,000 × 0% = $0 because the article is entered under the specified aluminum section 232 heading in note 52(f)(1); Case U also has the USMCA free-entry exception.
- Section 338: not yet effective before August 22, 2026; on August 25 and September 14 the original section 232 exclusion applies. From September 15, the motor-vehicles scope proclamation expressly makes section 338 additive to section 232.

*For Case N on March 14 and June 3, the $25,000 figure treats the now-unlawful IEEPA tariff as unable to trigger the old non-stacking rule. A materially different reading treats the historical entry as having been 'subject to' that tariff when entered, preserving the then-applicable section 232 waiver: that would yield $100,000 × 0% = $0 section 232 and a $0 additional-duty total for those two N entries. The Federal Register materials found do not resolve that retroactive interaction.
Q15.uncertainty: The FR reports the Supreme Court ruling and describes refund orders for unliquidated and nonfinal entries, but does not resolve whether an unlawful historical IEEPA assessment still triggers the retroactive non-stacking waiver for Case N on March 14 and June 3. Final liquidation and refund eligibility are also not supplied. The cited CBP notice says remaining section 232 duties are retained and collected, but does not specifically decide this interaction. The June 2026 Annex I-C preferential-content rule does not apply to these extrusions under the stated list assumptions.
